The /api/investigations/audit route re-exports the audits list: it takes no investigation id or filter and returns the 100 newest audit-log rows of the whole organization (action, resource type, outcome, severity and the acting user id as auditor) to any officer, so a path named for the audit of an investigation discloses the organization-wide activity trail and cannot show the audit of one investigation.

The knowledge-base list and item routes filter only by the organization and its parent and by is_active: they never read is_public or allowed_organizations, so the access-control columns of the table do not limit a read (the publish route stores exit-interview copies with is_public false and they are still returned), they apply no union_knowledge_suite entitlement although publication requires it, the list q parameter matches the full content of rows whose content it does not return (a search oracle over exit-interview text), and neither read writes an audit record of who opened which document.

The knowledge-base item GET writes: after the read it runs UPDATE knowledge_base SET view_count = view_count + 1 WHERE id under withSystemContext, which bypasses row-level security, with no organization predicate, not awaited and with no audit record; the id was matched under an organization predicate by the select just before, but the write itself is an unscoped system-context statement that a read-only route should not hold.

The geofence GET takes latitude and longitude from the query string and, when the point is inside the fence, checkGeofenceEntry inserts a geofence_events row with the member user id, the geofence id and the precise coordinates through the shared db handle, with no call to hasValidConsent, no tracking-enabled check, no transaction and no audit record, so a member who never opted in or revoked consent has a precise position stored by a GET, and that row can be neither read nor deleted through the consent routes (revocation answers 404 when no active consent exists).

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: Any signed-in user whose organization owns a geofence can call GET /api/location/geofence with that geofence id and a point inside it, and a geofence_events row with the user id and the coordinates is stored whether or not the user holds an active location consent; no web or mobile caller of the route exists in the repository, and the only deletion of such rows is the retention handler that no scheduler entry invokes.

potentialImpact.description: A client that checks geofence entry for members who have not opted in, or after revocation, records their precise position without the explicit opt-in the service header promises and without a trace in the audit trail, and the member has no route that erases those rows.

existingContainment.summary: The caller must belong to the organization that owns the geofence and the stored user id is the session user, so only the caller own position is stored; the row carries a 24-hour expiry that the retention handler, not the route, acts on.

releaseDisposition.blockingCondition: A web or mobile client calls the geofence entry check for a member who has no active location consent, or the location retention handler remains unscheduled while any client submits positions.
releaseDisposition.justification: The route stores a precise position on a GET with no consent condition, which contradicts the opt-in rule stated by the service; the data is the caller own and no client in the repository calls the route, so the release is blocked when a client submits positions for members without consent or without the retention job running.

defectRegister.title: The consent DELETE revokes consent and deletes the member location points and geofence events only after an update that matches a consent row whose status is not opted_out, and it answers 404 and deletes nothing when the member has no such row, so a member whose positions were stored without consent (geofence entry check), whose consent was revoked earlier, or who never had a consent row, has no route that erases the stored rows and depends on the retention handler that no scheduler invokes.

The location track POST inserts the precise position through the shared db handle with no transaction, no persistAtomicAudit, no location_tracking_audit row and no log of the write, although consent grant and revocation are audited, so no record shows when positions were collected for a member; getConfig creates a default configuration row with tracking enabled on first use as a side effect of this write path; and a missing consent, a disabled configuration and any database failure are all answered 500 with the raw error message.

The location consent row is unique by user id alone with no organization, strike or event column, and tracking checks only that an opted-in row exists plus the strike or event flag for strike, picket and event points: the free-text consentPurpose and the purpose description are never compared with the purpose of a point, meeting and organizing points need nothing beyond an opt-in, and strikeId and eventId are accepted as any uuid and not verified to belong to the organization, so a consent given for one purpose in one organization authorizes collection for every other purpose, strike and event.

The consent POST stores the consentText, purpose and purposeDescription exactly as the request body gives them, under a fixed consentVersion of 1.0: the zod schema declared for the route is never applied (the body is destructured unchecked and only checked for presence), the server holds no copy of the text the member was shown, and the same request can claim any text, so the stored consent record, which the privacy model calls the exact text shown to the user, is attested by the caller and not by the application.

The consent status GET calls hasValidConsent, which updates the consent row to expired through the shared db handle, with no transaction and no audit record, when the stored expiry has passed, and reflects the unvalidated context query parameter without checking that it is strike or event, so a read changes the consent state and leaves no trace.

The geofence POST applies no schema (the declared zod schema is unused): name, type, coordinates and radius are checked only for presence and simple comparisons on the raw body values, so a string coordinate passes the range checks and then fails at toFixed with a 500, the radius has no upper bound, so a geofence the size of the planet makes every position inside it, the geofence type is any text, and strikeId is stored without being verified to belong to the organization.

The /api/healthwelfare/plans route is the generic crudRoutes configuration over per_capita_remittances and has nothing to do with health and welfare plans: a GET returns the organization remittance ledger at the member floor (member counts, per-capita rate, total amount, approver and rejecter user ids, rejection reason, payment method and reference, remittance and receipt file URLs), and a POST is refused because the table is READ_ONLY in the CRUD governance table, so every member reads financial remittance records and no plan exists behind the name.

The /api/meeting-rooms/[id]/bookings route is the generic item configuration over meeting_rooms: its id is a room id and a GET returns the room row (not its bookings, which live in room_bookings and are read by nothing here), and a DELETE sent to a bookings path to cancel a booking removes the room itself at the administrator floor, so a client that treats the path as a booking collection cancels no booking and takes the room out of service.

The operational metrics GET admits any signed-in user of any organization, or any caller that presents the AI service key, and then counts claims, claim status changes in the last 24 hours, claims not closed that were last updated more than five days ago, and claim-update messages containing error or failed across every organization: requireApiAuth is called with no options (so no organization and no role is required), none of the four database reads carries an organization predicate, and they run through the shared database client outside any organization context, on a connection whose role the migration that introduced the runtime roles records as rolbypassrls = true, so row-level security does not narrow them.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: Any signed-in user of any organization, and any caller holding the AI service key, receives the platform-wide counts of claims, status changes, overdue claims and error-like claim updates from the route, with the figures of every organization added together and no organization narrowing.

potentialImpact.description: A member or steward of one organization learns the volume and workload of every other organization (how many claims exist, how many changed state in a day, how many are stale), which is cross-tenant disclosure of operational data that only a platform mandate could authorize, and no mandate is named in the source.

activationEvidence.quote: rolbypassrls = true, so it ignores RLS entirely regardless of what

releaseDisposition.justification: The route is reachable by any authenticated caller, the counts it returns are computed over every organization with no predicate, and the only database control that could narrow them is row-level security, which the recorded state of the connection role ignores; no role floor, entitlement or flag in the route limits who receives the figures, so the disclosure follows from the route as written.

defectRegister.title: The operational metrics GET names the lifetime claim count of all organizations request_count (its own header says request_count is a proxy that returns a placeholder), derives error_rate from the number of claim updates whose message contains the text error or failed divided by the number of status changes in 24 hours, and runs its five reads under Promise.allSettled so that a rejected read is replaced by 0 (or an empty queue list) and the response is still 200 with window 24h, so an unreachable database or job queue reads as a healthy zero and the figures are not request counts or error rates.

The operational metrics GET compares the x-service-key header with AI_SERVICE_KEY using ===, which is not a constant-time comparison (lib/api/secret-compare.ts holds secretsEqual for this purpose and the route does not use it), accepts that one shared key as authority over the figures of every organization, and when the data queries throw returns 500 with detail set to String(err), so the text of a database or queue error reaches every caller that passed the check.

The churn-risk routes score a named member with a TensorFlow network that has no trained weights in the repository: loadChurnModel reads model.json from disk and, when it is absent (no code calls saveChurnModel), builds a new network and fits it for 50 epochs on 150 generated examples whose feature values are drawn with Math.random from hand-written ranges (the medium-risk labels are Math.random() > 0.5 ? 1 : 0), the normalisation constants are literals and confidence is Math.abs(churnProbability - 0.5) * 2; the POST stores the result with isPredictionFromML true and returns it as aiGenerated with source ml, so a risk level for a named person is presented as the output of a trained model when it is the output of a randomly initialised network fitted on invented data, and the interventions derived from it (priority outreach, a dedicated steward) attach to that person.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: An officer of an organization can call the churn-risk routes; the POST names a member and computes a score through the randomly initialised network, stores it and returns it marked reviewRequired, and the GET lists stored scores with member names. The SQL names columns no schema file in the repository defines, so on a database built from the repository the statements are rejected before a score is stored or listed.

potentialImpact.description: An officer is shown a numeric risk level and recommended interventions for a named member that are produced by noise-fitted arithmetic and labelled as machine learning, which can lead to outreach or steward assignment decisions about a person on the basis of a figure that carries no information about that person.

existingContainment.summary: The response metadata marks the output aiGenerated and reviewRequired and the route is limited to the officer role floor, so a person is expected to review the score before acting; nothing in the route makes the review a condition of a stored score or of the interventions returned.

releaseDisposition.blockingCondition: The churn-risk SQL runs against a database that holds the profile, claim and prediction columns it names (or is repaired to run) while the model directory holds no trained weights, so that scores for named members are produced and stored by the synthetic network.
releaseDisposition.justification: Harm requires the statements to execute, which the repository schema does not support, so release is blocked only once they can: from that moment every score for a named member comes from a network fitted on generated examples and is presented as a model output with a confidence figure, and the reviewRequired flag does not prevent the score from being stored or returned.

defectRegister.title: The churn-risk SQL names columns and values that no schema file in the repository defines: the POST reads profiles.organization_id, full_name, union_tenure_years and member_age (profiles is the billing profile and has none of them) and claims.resolution_notes, counts claims with status withdrawn (a value the claim_status enum does not have) and inserts user_id, model_type, model_version, prediction_value, confidence_score, predicted_at, response_time_ms and features_used into ml_predictions, and the GET filters ml_predictions on model_type and predicted_at and joins profiles on user_id, while the declared ml_predictions shape, which the storage authority register calls canonical, has none of those columns, so on a database built from the repository these statements are rejected and the route answers 500 instead of a prediction; the intervention strings the POST stores and returns also carry garbled characters (UTF-8 emoji decoded as Latin-1 text).

The churn-risk routes build a risk profile of a named member from that member case history (claim count, resolution rate, days since the last claim, a satisfaction figure the SQL itself labels simulated and infers from claim status and a resolution-notes text match, and a count of withdrawn claims), store the case-derived features in ml_predictions.features_used and return the member name, risk score, contributing factors such as inactive for N days or N negative feedback incidents, and tenure to any officer, with no record of what members are told, whether they consented, which office may act on a score or how long a score is kept.

The churn-risk invocation audit is a separate write outside the data transaction and ahead of the checks that decide whether the call is valid: auditAIInvocation writes an audit_logs row through auditLog and its own tenant context before the GET checks the organization and before the POST validates the body, so a rejected request leaves an AI invocation record with outcome success, the GET (a read method) writes a row on every call, and the POST prediction row and its persistAtomicAudit record commit in a second, unrelated transaction; the auditRefId returned in the response metadata names the first record, not the committed prediction.

The churn-risk handlers are registered with withRoleAuth at the officer floor but ignore the context it supplies (the parameter is named _context) and resolve the user and organization a second time with getCurrentUser, the GET counts claims per member with a subquery (WHERE member_id = p.user_id) that carries no organization predicate and runs through the shared database client outside any organization context, the limit query parameter is parseInt of the raw string with no number check and no upper bound, and neither handler applies guardAiFeature although the sibling model routes apply one.

The SLA breach risk POST returns computeSlaBreachProbability, a sum of literal weights over four caller-supplied values (priority, hoursRemaining, transitionCount, hasPreviousBreaches; featureRefs is only required to be a list of strings of two characters or more), clamped to 0.01 to 0.99, together with a constant confidence 0.78, bounds of plus and minus 0.08 and a model object with type, version and trainedAt taken from a model_metadata row the route inserts with scoring heuristic_v1 when none exists, so arithmetic over unverified inputs is presented as a model prediction with a confidence and a training date, and a steward can obtain any score (including 0.80 and above, which the realtime alerting sweep counts as an imminent breach signal) by choosing the inputs.

The SLA breach risk POST accepts caseId as any GUID, never reads claims or grievances to check that it exists or belongs to the organization, and does not store it on the ml_predictions row (the table has no case column; the id appears only in the audit record details and the response), so a score is not attached to a case, the GET cannot list the predictions of a case, and the feedback route cannot check that a prediction belongs to the case it is later said to be about.

The SLA breach risk POST and feedback POST take modelVersion from the caller (default sla-risk-v1, any non-empty string), look up model_metadata by organization, type sla_breach_risk and that string, and insert a new model_metadata row when none exists (the POST with the caller featureRefs as parameters, the feedback with empty parameters), so a steward creates unbounded model rows, the version recorded for a prediction is whatever was typed, and feedback can be recorded against a version the prediction was never made with.

The SLA feedback POST lets a steward submit feedback for the same prediction any number of times (nothing records that a prediction already has feedback), takes actualBreach and resolutionHours from the request body with no check against the case, and folds each submission into a running mean absolute error by reading the model_metadata parameters JSON and writing it back without a row lock or version check, so two concurrent submissions overwrite one another observation count and a steward can move the quality score and the retrain recommendation at will.

The SLA feedback routes compute meanAbsoluteError, a qualityScore written to model_metadata.accuracy, retrainRecommended after 30 observations with an error above 0.25, a trainingDataQueue of the last 200 submissions (each with its free-text comment and submitting user id) and a retrainSignal, and the GET returns them as the model feedback summary, but no code reads trainingDataQueue or retrainSignal and the scoring function that produced the predictions is a fixed formula that never reads model parameters, so no retraining can follow from the signal and the accuracy figure describes a formula that stays as it is.

The SLA feedback POST updates model_metadata inside withRLSContext, which when UE_CANONICAL_BOOTSTRAP_V2 is 1 runs the transaction as the union_eyes_runtime role, and the round-58 migration revokes every privilege from that role on model_metadata and grants SELECT and INSERT only (the storage authority register records the same required privileges), so under that configuration the UPDATE is refused with a permission error, the whole transaction including the audit record rolls back and the steward receives a server error for every feedback submission, although the route is the one the register lists as the feedback path.

The SLA feedback POST calls trackPilotEvent after the transaction has committed and awaits it with no error handling: trackPilotEvent inserts into pilot_events through the shared database client imported from @/db outside any organization context (the route holds no tenant transaction at that point, and pilot_events carries a direct organization row-level policy), so when that insert fails the steward receives an error for feedback that was already committed and audited, and a retry records the observation a second time; the pilot_events activity record is therefore written in a separate transaction from the feedback and its atomic audit record, so the audit trail of the submission is split across two commits that can disagree.

The SLA breach risk GET lists the latest 25 stored sla_breach_risk prediction rows of the organization at the member floor with no guardAiFeature feature gate and no enforceAISafety call (the destructured handler argument is only organizationId), where the POST of the same file and both methods of the feedback route apply both, so an organization that has switched the AI feature off still serves its stored predictions to every member.

The ml/query POST forwards the free-text question of a steward (up to 500 characters), an arbitrary context value validated only as z.any(), the organization id and the shared AI_SERVICE_TOKEN bearer to the service at AI_SERVICE_URL, and merges the JSON the service returns (which its own contract says may include the generated sql and result data) into the response unfiltered, with no record of what the service may receive, no data-class or consent decision and no check of what comes back, while nothing in the repository implements the /api/query endpoint to show that it applies the organization id it is sent; the question and context can name members and cases.

The ml/query POST records its audit through logApiAuditEvent, which only writes a logger.info line (the question cut to 100 characters and the confidence), after the external call and not persisted, and it calls enforceAISafety with userRole member and dataClass internal although the route requires steward and answers over claims, steward workload and settlement data; enforceAISafety reads only the user id, organization id, requested entity organization and canMutate, so the declared role and data class are labels and not controls, and a question that is answered leaves no durable audit record.

The ml/monitoring/metrics GET queries ml_predictions for predicted_at, prediction_correct and assignment_accepted and model_metadata for model_name, precision, recall, f1_score, last_evaluated_at, baseline_accuracy and baseline_confidence, none of which the declared tables have, and joins model_metadata to the per-model figures on model_name with no organization predicate (the table is organization-scoped, and the query runs through the shared database client rather than a tenant transaction), so on a database built from the repository the route fails with a column error, and were the columns present the join would mix the model rows of every organization into one organization figures.

The ml/monitoring/metrics GET substitutes literal figures for what was not measured and reports them as model health: precision, recall and f1 are COALESCEd to 0.80, the status CASE returns critical whenever accuracy is NULL and healthy only at 0.85 and above, and the mapping code turns a missing value into 0, a missing status into healthy, a missing trend into stable and a missing last_evaluated_at into the current time, so a model with no measurements is reported with 0.80 quality figures and a fresh timestamp.

The drift, usage, claim-outcome, timeline, workload-forecast and recommendations routes are the same generic crudRoutes configuration over ml_predictions, so each lists every stored prediction row of the organization whatever its type (page of 50, at most 100) and inserts a caller-supplied row, while its name advertises drift monitoring, usage monitoring, an outcome prediction, a timeline forecast, a workload forecast or recommendations, and nothing is computed, filtered by type or monitored behind any of them.

A steward can insert an ml_predictions row of any prediction type, value, bounds, confidence and horizon through the six generic prediction routes (the body is copied into the insert), and the same table is what the SLA breach risk list returns for type sla_breach_risk, what the SLA feedback route accepts a prediction id from, what the realtime alerting sweep counts under withSystemContext (sla_breach_risk rows from the last 60 minutes with predicted_value at or above 0.80, which raises an organization alert) and what the insights generator reads as the latest 20 predictions, so a caller-chosen row is stored with no provenance and is consumed as a model output.

The declared ml_predictions shape (prediction_type, prediction_date, predicted_value, bounds, confidence, horizon, granularity) conflicts with the SQL files that create the table: db/migrations/20260324_add_remaining_missing_tables.sql, db/migrations/20260507_fixup_create_break_glass_activations.sql and db/migrations/manual/067_advanced_analytics_q1_2025.sql each create it with model_name, model_version and target_date NOT NULL and no default, and migrations-platform/0019 only adds the declared columns (and sets NOT NULL on them only when the table is empty), so on a table created from those files the inserts of the SLA breach risk route and of the generic prediction routes, which supply none of the legacy columns, are refused by the database.

The ml/monitoring/alerts routes name columns and a table that the repository does not define and the GET holds SQL that is not valid: it reads ml_predictions.model_type, predicted_at, prediction_correct and confidence_score (the declared table has prediction_type, prediction_date and confidence), joins a table ml_alert_acknowledgments that no schema file or migration creates, ends two SELECT lists with a trailing comma before FROM and orders by alert_timestamp, which no CTE selects, so the GET answers 500 and the POST, which inserts into ml_alert_acknowledgments, fails with a missing relation, on a database built from the repository.

The ml/monitoring/alerts GET emits a P1 finding with the literal text Data drift detected: Case Complexity PSI = 0.28 (threshold: 0.25) for Claim Outcome Prediction whenever the organization has created more than 100 claims in the last 7 days, whatever the data is (no population stability index is computed), and builds every alert id from the model type and TO_CHAR(NOW(), YYYYMMDDHH24MISS), so a drift figure is asserted from claim volume alone and the id of each alert changes every second, so an alert cannot be referred to twice.

The ml/monitoring/alerts POST requires alertId to be z.guid, while every id the GET generates is text such as perf_<model>_<timestamp>, so no listed alert can be acknowledged; the insert is keyed ON CONFLICT (alert_id) alone, so an acknowledgement of one alert id by one organization blocks the same id for every other organization (the update applies only to the organization own row and a conflict is answered 409), and the POST accepts any GUID the caller types, acknowledging an alert that does not exist.

The ml/monitoring/alerts GET joins ml_alert_acknowledgments on alert_id with no organization predicate and runs the whole read through the shared database client rather than a tenant transaction (the POST uses withRLSContext), so an acknowledgement written by another organization for the same alert id would be shown as acknowledged, with the acknowledging user id and time, in this organization list.

The /api/metrics route is a generic crudRoutes configuration over analytics_metrics that lists the organization stored metric rows at the member floor and accepts a steward-supplied row, while lib/observability/metrics.ts documents the Prometheus (prom-client) metrics as available at GET /api/metrics and lib/public-routes.ts names /api/metrics as a role-scoped infrastructure route, so a scraper pointed at the documented path receives JSON rows of business metric records (including their metadata column) rather than metrics in the exposition format.

The /api/movement-insights/trends route is a generic crudRoutes configuration over analytics_metrics (the organization own metric rows, readable at the member floor and insertable by a steward), while the movement insights dashboard page documents anonymized cross-union trends with a minimum of 5 organizations per trend, no individual organization identifiable and a consent status, reads movementTrends and dataAggregationConsent, and admits only the MOVEMENT_INSIGHTS_ROLES office list, so the API path serves none of the consent, minimum-population or office controls its name and its dashboard describe and returns organization rows under a movement-trends name.

The notification list GET wraps its three queries in a try block whose catch logs and returns an empty notifications array, unreadCount 0 and zero totals as a normal 200 (the comment says the in_app_notifications table may lack expected columns), and a non-numeric page parameter becomes NaN, fails the query and takes the same path; the count GET catches every error with an empty catch and returns count 0; so a failed read is shown to the member as no notifications and no unread items, and the dashboard top bar that calls the count route cannot tell the two apart.

The notification create POST lets a steward insert a row for any non-deleted member of the organization with a caller-written title, message, type, action label, action url and data object taken from an unvalidated body (no schema, no length or shape bound, an unparsable expiresAt becomes an Invalid Date that fails at insert and answers 500), and in_app_notifications has no created-by or sender column and the insert sets none, so the recipient sees a steward-authored message in the same inbox and with the same presentation as a system notification; the acting steward appears only in the audit record, whose details hold the recipient and type but not the text, and nothing limits which members or how often.

The notification PATCH reads read from the body without a schema: a value that is truthy but not a boolean (such as the string false) sets readAt to now and stores the text in the boolean column, a value PostgreSQL cannot parse as a boolean fails at the update and answers 500, and setting read to false never clears readAt, so the stored read timestamp can contradict the flag; the audit record stores the raw read value that was sent.

The notification test POST inserts one in-app row for the calling steward with a fixed title and the message that it verifies that the notification setup is working correctly, but it calls no push, e-mail or SMS channel and reads no device or preference, so a success proves only that a database row was written; every call adds another row with no expiry and no de-duplication, and the response is the stored row, not a delivery result.

The push device collection reads at the member floor and restricts a read to the caller own profile, but its POST requires the steward floor, so a member (the only person who holds the phone) is refused with 403 when the retired /api/notifications/device route sends them to /api/mobile/devices to register; for a steward the insert copies every body field into push_devices apart from the forced profileId (enabled, quiet hours, timezone, lastActiveAt, id, createdAt), an unknown platform value fails the push_platform enum and a user without a profiles row fails the foreign key, both as 500.

Devices are kept in two unrelated tables: push_devices (written by the generic device route) and mobile_devices (written by the sync route), each with its own token, preference and active columns, and neither route exports a PATCH or DELETE or has an item route, so a device or token can never be disabled, archived or removed by its owner or an administrator, a device that passes to another account is refused with 409 by the ownership check on every later registration, and the only code that reads either table for delivery (services/fcm-service.ts over push_devices and lib/mobile/mobile-engine.ts over mobile_devices) is imported by no route, worker or script outside its tests.

The mobile sync GET selects every column of mobile_devices and the POST returns the inserted row, and the device collection GET and POST return the whole push_devices row, so each response carries the device push token (a delivery credential for that device) together with the jailbreak flag, compliance issues, last compliance check and metadata columns; the rows are limited to the caller own devices, but nothing projects the token or the security flags out of a response that a browser or script can read.

The /api/mobile/sync route lists and registers mobile devices and synchronizes nothing: it never touches the mobile_sync_queue table that the mobile engine defines, and its POST refuses a body without deviceToken, deviceId and platform, while the only in-repository caller, the Sync now button in SyncStatus, posts just deviceId (or the text unknown) and platform pwa with no deviceToken, so that request is always answered 400 and the control reports an error whatever the device state.

When the same user posts an existing deviceId the sync POST updates deviceToken, appVersion, osVersion and lastActiveAt but not organizationId, so a user who registers the device while acting in a second organization receives the row still bound to the first organization (the GET filters by the current organization and will not list it) while the audit record is written for the second one; a deviceToken already held by a different deviceId, and a platform, name or version longer than its varchar column, are not checked and surface as raw database constraint failures answered 500.

The /api/mobile/push/subscribe and /api/mobile/push/unsubscribe routes are the same crudRoutes configuration over push_notifications, the push campaign table: the browser client posts the PushSubscription (endpoint and keys) to subscribe and { endpoint } to unsubscribe, neither of which names the NOT NULL campaign columns, so a steward request fails at insert and answers 500 and a member request is refused 403 at the steward floor, no subscription or opt-out is ever stored or removed, and the client never inspects the status, so it marks the browser subscribed after subscribe and unsubscribed after unsubscribe although the server did nothing.

The push campaign GET paths return the push_notifications rows of the organization to any member (member read floor, no owner column, and the table has no user column for the low-role guard to apply), including draft and scheduled campaigns with their name, title and body, targeting (target type, target criteria with roles, statuses, tags and custom fields, topics), the uuid array of targeted push_devices rows, delivery counters and the creating user id, so every member can read unpublished union campaigns and how they are aimed.

The push campaign POST copies the whole request body into push_notifications at the steward floor, so a steward can create a row with status sent, sentAt, targetType all and any totalTargeted, totalSent, totalDelivered, totalClicked and totalDismissed values, and the row then reads as a delivered campaign with engagement figures although no route, worker or script that is imported by the application sends a push (services/fcm-service.ts has no importer outside its tests) and no push_deliveries row exists.

The /api/mobile/notifications route is the generic factory over the notifications table (the scheduled deadline-reminder queue: type, priority, related entity, scheduled time and send status), not the in_app_notifications inbox that /api/notifications serves, so a mobile client that lists notifications receives a different dataset with no read flag or read route; a member sees only their own rows but a steward or above reads every user scheduled notification of the organization, with message text and the related grievance, claim or deadline reference.

The scheduled-notification POST copies the body into the notifications table at the steward floor with no check that the target userId is a member of the organization (the sibling /api/notifications POST makes that check), so a steward can store a row addressed to any user id string, set its status to sent and its sentAt, priority and related entity, and that row reads as a delivered notification although the notification-processing cron that would send scheduled rows answers 501 NOT_IMPLEMENTED.

The top-level /api/negotiations route is a second copy of the /api/bargaining/negotiations collection: the crudRoutes configuration over the negotiations table is identical in both files (member read, steward write, organization scoped, no blockedPatchFields), so the same confidential negotiation records are reachable by two paths and a role, confidentiality or field restriction added to one path leaves the other open.

The negotiation POST lets a steward store strikeVotePassed, strikeVoteDate, strikeVoteYesPercent, mandateExpiry, estimatedCost, maximumCost, status and confidentialityLevel from the request body, and the route reads no vote, poll, mandate or costing record to verify them, so a steward-typed strike-vote result or cost ceiling is stored as the negotiation record and is then returned to every member by the member-floor GET.

meeting_rooms rows store requiresApproval, allowedUserRoles, blockedDates, operatingHours, min and max booking duration and advanceBookingDays, and the room routes let stewards set them, but no route reads or writes room_bookings and the only booking code, lib/services/calendar-service.ts, returns true from checkRoomAvailability and builds an in-memory booking with the comment that production would insert into room_bookings, so a room configured to require approval or to exclude a role enforces neither and a booking is never stored.

A PATCH sent to /api/meeting-rooms/[id]/bookings updates the meeting_rooms row whose id is the path value at the steward floor, copying every body field except the primary key and the organization (status, isActive, requiresApproval, allowedUserRoles, blockedDates, contact person, e-mail and phone, imageUrl, metadata, createdAt), and reads or changes no room_bookings row, so a client that patches a booking changes the room itself and a booking id addresses nothing.

The four OCI routes (intake, assessment, results and report) are wrappers over the OCRA alias handlers, which re-export the ICRA handlers, and each wrapper calls a local requireOrgAccess function that returns the literal true for every request and, for the intake and assessment POST, a validateMutationBoundary whose schema checks only that request.method is a string, so the 401 and 400 branches are unreachable and the file reads as an organization access check over a flow that is in fact anonymous and authorized only by the assessment bearer capability; the OCI paths add a third public name for the same handlers, with the same limits, consent gaps and defects, and no behaviour of their own.

The OCRA e-mail results path re-exports the ICRA e-mail results handler, which accepts any syntactically valid address typed by the caller, with no proof that the caller controls it, and sends a branded message from the platform through the e-mail provider that embeds the caller 30-day bearer capability in the link fragment, so any holder of a capability (the start path issues one to anyone) can make the platform mail the capability link to a third party under a second public path name, limited only by the per-process in-memory allowance, and no decision names who may receive an assessment link.

The peer benchmarks route (member floor) takes the organization to benchmark from the organizationId query parameter and the clause suggestions route (officer floor) takes it from the organizationId body field, and both handlers destructure the session organization as an unused underscore variable and never compare it with the requested id, so the library reads whichever organizations row the request names (and, for benchmarks, the member counts of its peers) and the only boundary left is the row-level-security policy on the organizations table, which the route cannot show was applied to the connection it ran on; a request that names another organization returns that organization data wherever the policy does not hide the row.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: Any member of any organization can call the peer benchmarks route and any officer can call the clause suggestions route with an organization id of their choice, because both handlers discard the session organization and pass the requested id to the library; what comes back depends only on which organizations rows the database context lets the query see.

potentialImpact.description: Where the policy does not hide the requested organization, a member of one organization would read another organization member count, its peer average and percentile, and a clause list shaped by its sector, province and hierarchy path, which are organization data that the caller session does not entitle them to.

activationEvidence.quote: export const GET = withRoleAuth('member' as MemberRole, async (request, context) => {

existingContainment.summary: The organizations table carries a direct organization policy so that a tenant transaction sees only its own row, and the db import used by the library resolves to the active tenant transaction, so with a connection role that the policy constrains the lookup of another organization finds no row and the library returns an empty list.

evidence.quote: SELECT ue_create_direct_org_rls_policy('organizations', 'id', FALSE); -- a tenant sees only its own org row

releaseDisposition.blockingCondition: The database role that runs these queries is not constrained by the organizations policy (a role with BYPASSRLS, a superuser, or a connection that does not carry the tenant context the policy expects), or the organizations policy is relaxed to expose hierarchy or peer rows.
releaseDisposition.justification: The routes themselves enforce nothing about whose organization is named and any member or officer can reach them, so the exposure rests entirely on a database policy that the source does not prove is applied to the connection in use; the harm is real disclosure of another organization data if that single control does not hold, which is a condition of the deployment and not of the route, so release is blocked wherever the connection role can read organizations rows other than the caller own.

defectRegister.title: The federation discovery route (officer floor) passes a province, a sector and a member-count estimate from the body to a query over every active organization of type federation or congress, ordered by member count and limited to 10, with no organization predicate, and returns each match with its id, name, organization type, province and member count, so an officer of any organization is offered a directory of other organizations by design, and the only thing that narrows it is the organizations row-level-security policy that lets a tenant transaction see its own row; no source decides what a prospective affiliate may see of a federation.

The functions behind federation discovery, peer benchmarks and clause suggestions wrap their whole body in a try that logs the error and returns an empty array, and the peer benchmark and clause suggestion lookups throw Organization not found for an id they cannot see before that catch, so a database failure, an unknown or invisible organization id and a genuine absence of matches all reach the route as an empty list and are answered 200 with success true and a total of 0, and the caller cannot tell a refused or failed lookup from an empty result.

The federation matching function accepts a sector and never reads it (the route documents matching on sector and the filters use only organization type, status and province), adds the reason Similar size category whenever both member counts exist whatever their ratio (the score term is the ratio times 20, but the reason is pushed for a ratio of 0.001 as for 0.9), and awards fixed weights of 40, 30, 20 and 10 points, so the matchScore and matchReasons shown to the officer as grounds for choosing a parent federation are literals that do not follow from the data they name.

The clause suggestion scorer awards 40 points to federation-shared clauses and 50 to congress-level templates and lists the source organization name from the sourceOrganization relation, while the shared clause library policy deliberately gives federation and congress sharing levels no visibility beyond owner, shared-with or public and the organizations policy lets a tenant see only its own row, so those weights can apply only to rows the policy shows (owned, shared with the organization or public), every other source name resolves to Unknown, the sector and province bonuses are added to rows that the filters already restricted to the same sector and province, and the relevance reasons shown to the officer describe a federation hierarchy the data access does not provide.

The peer benchmark function obtains the national average through fetchNationalAverage, which returns the literal table from getFallbackAverage (member count 2500, per-capita rate 45, staff 8, budget 1250000, grievance resolution 45 days) when CLC_API_KEY is unset, when the CLC API answers 404 or an unexpected body, and on any thrown error, and the route returns it as nationalAverage with no flag that it is a fallback; the peer average is computed as a sum divided by the count of peers with a positive member count, which is 0 divided by 0 when every peer has none, and nationalAverage falls back to the peer average when null.

The smart defaults route returns recommended features, suggested integrations and suggested API, document and storage limits from literal tables keyed on an unvalidated organizationType query value (any unknown value falls back to the local table) and a member count taken with parseInt (NaN, zero and negative values are treated as the default of 100), and the feature and integration names, for example benchmark-suite, cross-federation-collaboration, inter-union-messaging, provincial-lrb, wage-data and microsoft-365, appear in no other source file of the repository while no code reads the suggested limits, so the response presents hard-coded suggestions as intelligent defaults for capabilities that no route, registry or limiter defines.

The federation discovery, peer benchmarks and clause suggestions routes record their audit trail with eventBus.emit(AppEvents.AUDIT_LOG, ...) after the work is done, an in-memory event bus whose only retained state is a 1000-entry history, and no code anywhere in the application subscribes to system.audit_log, so no audit row is ever written for these reads of other organization data, the emitted event carries no organization id of the actor, and the comment Emit audit event describes a record that does not exist.

The onboarding events route lets any steward or higher write a pilot event and an atomic audit row named onboarding.event.org_created, onboarding.event.user_invited or onboarding.event.role_assigned for a targetUserId and role that are free strings in the body, without creating the organization, sending an invitation or changing any role and without checking that the target user belongs to the organization or that the role exists, so the pilot event table and the audit log hold attestations that a milestone happened which the caller merely asserted.

The onboarding events payload accepts metadata as an unbounded record of unknown values and the handler spreads it after targetUserId and role when it builds the stored pilot event metadata, so a caller can overwrite the targetUserId and role of the event row with different values than the ones the audit row records, and the same unbounded object is written twice (event metadata and audit details) with no size or key limit.

The onboarding transfers path advertises a transfer operation but is a wrapper that calls the onboarding events recorder behind a requireOrgAccess function that returns the literal true and a validateMutationBoundary that checks only that request.method is a string, so a POST to /api/onboarding/transfers records an org_created, user_invited or role_assigned event for the session organization (the event type enum has no transfer value) and the unreachable 401 and 400 branches read as an access check that is not there; the transfers page route only redirects to the pilot onboarding dashboard.

The onboarding root route is the generic CRUD factory over pending_profiles, the pre-signup profile table keyed by e-mail with the Whop membership id and usage credits, which the CRUD governance table lists as DENIED, so every GET and POST answers 403 before any query, while the SelfServeOnboarding component posts the organization name, type, province, plan and terms acceptance to /api/onboarding and navigates to the dashboard only when the response is ok (a refusal is silent), so the onboarding form has no route that can accept it and the path name does not describe the table behind it.

The onboarding root route sets orgScoped true over pending_profiles, which has no organization column, so the factory adds no tenant predicate: a GET at the support_agent floor would list the pre-signup e-mail, Whop membership id, billing cycle and credit balances of every organization and a POST at the steward floor would insert a profile from the request body; the DENIED entry in the CRUD governance table is the only barrier, and the continuity inheritance route is a second path over the same table, so one governance entry guards both.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: The onboarding root route and its readiness alias are reachable by a support_agent (read) or a steward (write) of any organization, but the CRUD governance table lists pending_profiles as DENIED, so the factory refuses every read and write with 403 before any query and no row is returned or written today.

potentialImpact.description: If the governance entry changes, the pre-signup e-mail addresses, Whop membership identifiers, billing cycle dates and credit balances of every organization would be listable by any support_agent and insertable by any steward, because orgScoped on a table with no organization column filters nothing.

existingContainment.summary: pending_profiles is in the DENIED list of the CRUD governance table and the generic factory calls assertCrudRead and assertCrudWrite, which refuse a DENIED table with 403 before any query or insert.

releaseDisposition.blockingCondition: The pending_profiles entry is removed from the DENIED list of the CRUD governance table, or any route serves the table through the generic factory with orgScoped on a table that has no organization column.
releaseDisposition.justification: The table has no organization column so the route can never scope a read to a tenant, and one governance entry is the only thing between a role-floor caller and every organization pre-signup payment identifiers; no row is exposed while the entry stands, so the harm needs the entry to change, which makes the disposition conditional on that change and not on any property of the caller.

defectRegister.title: The onboarding readiness path advertises an onboarding readiness check but is a wrapper that calls the onboarding root handlers, the generic CRUD factory over pending_profiles, behind a requireOrgAccess function that returns the literal true and a validateMutationBoundary that checks only that request.method is a string, so no readiness is computed anywhere, every GET and POST is refused 403 by the DENIED governance entry, and the unreachable 401 and 400 branches read as an access check that is not there.

GET /api/organizations/[id] checks only that a session user id exists, validates only the uuid shape of the path id, and reads the organizations row of that id inside withSystemContext (the union_eyes_system role that the 0108 policy for the organizations table exempts), so any signed-in user receives the whole record of any organization: contact email, phone, website and address, charter number, subscription tier, billing contact id, the settings JSON, enabled features, member counts, creator id and legacy organization id, with no membership, role or mandate check.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: Any signed-in user can request /api/organizations/<uuid> for an organization that is not theirs: the handler checks only that a session user id exists, reads the row under withSystemContext and returns the mapped record including contact fields, billing contact id, settings and enabled features; the administrative dashboard pages call the same path for organizations the administrator picks.

potentialImpact.description: A member of one organization can read the contact details, billing contact reference, settings JSON (per-capita rate and fiscal configuration keys) and subscription tier of every other organization whose id they obtain, which the 0108 row-level-security policy states a tenant must not see.

releaseDisposition.justification: The only checks are a session user id and the uuid shape of the id; the read deliberately runs with the system role that bypasses the tenant policy and returns every column the mapper exposes, so a signed-in user of any organization reaches the record of any other. A cross-tenant read of contact, billing and settings data is not made acceptable by the id being hard to guess, so the route blocks release.

defectRegister.title: After the organization row is read inside withSystemContext, GET /api/organizations/[id] computes activeClaims, totalClaims and childCount with db.execute outside any withRLSContext or withSystemContext callback, so the grievances and organizations statements run on the pooled connection with no app.current_org_id set: under the 0108 tenant policy they return no rows (so the counts are zero for every organization, including the caller own), and on a connection role that bypasses the policy they return the real counts of whatever organization id the caller named; the route returns either an unisolated or a silently zero figure and cannot be relied on for either.

PATCH /api/organizations/[id] reads the request body with an unguarded req.json() and copies name, slug, display_name, email, phone, website, sectors and settings into the update with no schema validation: the settings JSON column (which holds per-capita rate, remittance day and fiscal year keys) is replaced wholesale by whatever object the organization administrator sends, a changed slug is accepted with no uniqueness or format check although the path route resolves organizations by slug, a malformed JSON body or an invalid sectors value surfaces as an unhandled 500, and the unvalidated email and website are stored as sent.

When a system administrator changes parent_id through PATCH /api/organizations/[id], the update writes only parentId: hierarchy_path and hierarchy_level of the organization and of every descendant are not recomputed, the new parent is not checked to exist or not to be a descendant of the organization, and no source in the route or its audit record keeps the previous parent, so the ancestors, descendants and path reads (which follow hierarchy_path) disagree with the children read (which follows parent_id) after a parent change.

DELETE /api/organizations/[id] lets the administrator of an organization set the status of that organization to archived with no further check, although the PATCH on the same route refuses any change of status unless the caller is a system administrator because lifecycle status defines the institution standing: the delete takes no reason or confirmation, does not look at child organizations (the parent_id foreign key restricts deletion, not archiving), does not require a second approver, and the archived status removes the organization from the canonical organization choices (only status active organizations are offered) and from the billing scheduler, so one organization administrator can take the whole organization out of service.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: A member of the organization with the admin role (or above) calls DELETE on the id of their own organization: requireUserForOrganization admits the member, the role check requires admin, and the update sets status archived and commits the organization.archive audit row in the same transaction; the PATCH on the same file refuses a status change unless requireSystemAdmin passes.

potentialImpact.description: The organization is withdrawn from organization selection and billing by one administrator, contradicting the route own rule that lifecycle status changes require platform governance; only a system administrator PATCH can restore the status.

activationEvidence.quote: return NextResponse.json({ error: 'Forbidden: requires admin role' }, { status: 403 })

existingContainment.summary: The caller must be a member of the organization with the admin role, the update touches only the path organization row inside the caller tenant transaction, an organization.archive audit row commits with it, and the change is a status value a system administrator can reverse through PATCH.

releaseDisposition.blockingCondition: The deployment runs the canonical organization selection (UE_CANONICAL_BOOTSTRAP_V2 set to 1), where only organizations with status active are offered, or the institution decides that archiving an organization is a platform governance act, as the PATCH on the same route already enforces.
releaseDisposition.justification: The harm is bounded to the organization of an administrator and is recorded in an atomic audit row, so it does not block while archived organizations remain usable; it blocks as soon as archived status removes the organization from selection or the institution reserves lifecycle status to platform governance, because the delete path then performs the act the update path refuses.

defectRegister.title: The organization-scoped guard that the item and roster routes call (requireUserForOrganization, through getUserContextForOrganization) finds the caller membership with only the user id and the organization id in the where clause, with no status and no deleted_at condition, so in the legacy (non-canonical) mode a member whose status is suspended or inactive, or whose row is soft-deleted, still passes as a member of the organization with the role the row keeps: they can read the full roster, update or archive the organization when the kept role is admin, and add roster members when it is steward or above; other lookups in organization-utils require status active.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: A person whose membership row is suspended, inactive or soft-deleted but still carries a role calls the roster or item routes of that organization: getUserContextForOrganization selects the membership by user id and organization id alone and returns its role, so the role floors of the routes are evaluated against a row the organization may have withdrawn.

potentialImpact.description: A removed or suspended steward or administrator keeps the authority of the kept role over roster reads and writes, organization updates and archiving until the row is deleted for good, and a removed member keeps read access to the roster with contact details.

releaseDisposition.blockingCondition: The deployment runs in the legacy mode (UE_CANONICAL_BOOTSTRAP_V2 unset or 0) and an organization holds a membership row with a suspended, inactive or deleted state that keeps a steward, admin or member role; the canonical mode resolves the role from the canonical organization context instead.
releaseDisposition.justification: The guard is the sole authority check of the roster and item routes and it accepts a withdrawn membership, so any organization that retains a role on a suspended or soft-deleted row gives that person live authority; the condition is a runtime mode and a data state the route file does not state, so the defect blocks release where both hold.

defectRegister.title: GET /api/organizations/[id]/members requires only that the caller is a member of the path organization (any role, including member, in any status) and returns every roster row with user id, name, email, phone, department, membership number, role, status, primary flag and join dates, with no role floor, no member-directory policy (the organization/members route limits stewards to members of their assigned cases and withholds employment data below officer), no pagination and no read audit; the page and the SMS campaign builder call it.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: Any member of an organization, whatever their role, calls /api/organizations/<own organization id>/members and receives the email, phone, membership number, role and status of every roster row of the organization; the same table is served to stewards through the narrower directory policy by organization/members, which this route does not apply.

potentialImpact.description: Contact details and membership numbers of every colleague, including those of members who have not consented to being listed, reach an ordinary member who has no case or office that needs them, which the sibling directory route is written to prevent.

releaseDisposition.justification: The membership check proves only that the caller belongs to the organization; no role floor or directory policy narrows what a member receives, so the personal contact data of the whole roster is reachable by every authenticated member today and the route blocks release.

defectRegister.title: GET /api/organizations/[id]/members selects every organization_members row of the organization with no deleted_at condition, no status filter, no limit and no ordering, so soft-deleted members are returned beside active ones with their contact details and the whole roster of a large organization is returned in one response, whereas organization/members excludes deleted rows.

POST /api/organizations/[id]/members lets any member whose role is steward or above insert an organization_members row for any user_id string with any of the roles member, steward, admin, executive or observer and an immediately active status: the route does not compare the granted role with the role of the caller, does not check that the user id exists or consented, does not use an invitation or acceptance step, and the inserted row is what getUserContextForOrganization later reads as the role of that person, so a steward can create an administrator or executive membership for an accomplice account; the unique (organization, user) index turns a repeated or previously removed user id into an unhandled 500.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: A steward of an organization posts a JSON body with any user_id and role admin to the roster of their own organization: the route validates the shape with zod, inserts the active membership with that role in the tenant transaction and commits a membership.create audit row, and the role it stores is the one the organization item routes then honour for that user.

potentialImpact.description: A steward can confer a higher organization role than they hold on any account, which then administers the organization (profile, settings, archive, roster), and adds people to the roster without their acceptance, exposing their contact data to the organization.

activationEvidence.quote: return NextResponse.json({ error: 'Forbidden: requires steward role' }, { status: 403 });

existingContainment.summary: The caller must be a member of the organization with at least the steward role, the body is validated by a zod schema that limits the role to five values and the email to a valid address, the insert is scoped to the path organization in its own transaction, and a membership.create audit row commits with it.

releaseDisposition.justification: The containment limits who can post but not what they may confer: the role enum includes admin and executive and no comparison with the caller role exists, so a steward can create authority above their own for any user id. This is a privilege-escalation path inside the tenant and blocks release until the granting office and the role ceiling are decided.

defectRegister.title: POST /api/organizations/[id]/members inserts without a conflict clause or an existence check, so a user id that already has a row (including a soft-deleted one) violates unique_org_membership and the exception propagates as an unhandled 500 rather than a 409, and the response of a successful insert returns the whole stored row including the generated ids.

The member directory projection used by GET /api/organization/members substitutes the department Administration and the position Union Member when the stored values are empty and reports seniority 0 for an officer-level reader when none is recorded, so the response presents canned organizational facts and an unmeasured seniority as recorded data about a member.

GET /api/organization/members/search places the raw q parameter inside an ILIKE pattern with no escaping of percent and underscore and no length bound, returns at most 50 rows with no ordering and no paging parameter so members past the first 50 matches are unreachable and the page returned is not stable, and returns the email address of each match to the caller.

GET /api/org/current is described as the canonical organization endpoint but reads no table: it returns the session organization id with name null, slug null, subscriptionTier null and an empty features list, and an availableOrgs array that holds only that same placeholder, so a client receives a 200 organization payload that carries none of the organization data and lists no other organization the user belongs to.

GET /api/organizations/current requires only a session user and returns the whole organization row of the session organization to any member, whatever their role: settings JSON (per-capita rate and fiscal configuration), billing_contact_id, subscription tier, enabled features, created_by, legacy_org_id, contact email and phone and the claim counts, none of which an ordinary member is shown to need.

GET /api/organizations/hierarchy lets any signed-in user list up to 500 organizations of every tenant (all organization types except platform) because it reads the organizations table inside withSystemContext with no membership, role or mandate check, and returns for each one the name, slug, type, parent id, hierarchy path and level, member count, active member count, child count, status, sectors and CLC affiliation; the rootOrgId query parameter only filters the rows already read, so it narrows nothing for a caller who leaves it out or names another organization, and the member counts are aggregate figures of organizations other than the caller own.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: Any signed-in user can call the route with the id of an organization that is not theirs: the only guard is the presence of a session user id, the lookup runs under withSystemContext (the union_eyes_system role that the 0108 row-level-security policy exempts), and the response returns the name, structure, member counts and affiliation of up to 500 organizations of that organization.

potentialImpact.description: A member or officer of one organization learns the identity, size and structure of organizations they have no relationship with; the 0108 policy states that a tenant sees only its own organization row, and this route discloses the name, structure, member counts and affiliation of up to 500 organizations outside that boundary.

releaseDisposition.justification: The route authenticates a user but never relates the caller to the requested organization, runs the read with the system role that bypasses tenant isolation, and returns the name, structure, member counts and affiliation of up to 500 organizations; a reachable cross-tenant read is not made safe by the data being organization-level, so the route blocks release until a mandate and a scope are decided.

defectRegister.title: GET /api/organizations/hierarchy sets rls_enabled to the constant true on every row whatever the policy state of the connection that read it (the read ran with the system role that the policy exempts), and truncates the list at 500 rows with no flag, total or page, so the child_count of a row is computed only from the truncated set and the response presents a complete and isolated tree it did not build.

GET /api/organizations/[id]/children reads every organization whose parent_id equals the path id inside withSystemContext after checking only that a session user exists, so any signed-in user can list the child organizations of any organization (including a federation or the congress) with name, slug, type, parent id, hierarchy path and level, sectors, member and active member counts, status, CLC affiliation and creation date; the scope is the path id and never the caller organization.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: Any signed-in user can call the route with the id of an organization that is not theirs: the only guard is the presence of a session user id, the lookup runs under withSystemContext (the union_eyes_system role that the 0108 row-level-security policy exempts), and the response returns the child organizations with their member counts, sectors, CLC affiliation and creation date of that organization.

potentialImpact.description: A member or officer of one organization learns the identity, size and structure of organizations they have no relationship with; the 0108 policy states that a tenant sees only its own organization row, and this route discloses the child organizations with their member counts, sectors, CLC affiliation and creation date outside that boundary.

releaseDisposition.justification: The route authenticates a user but never relates the caller to the requested organization, runs the read with the system role that bypasses tenant isolation, and returns the child organizations with their member counts, sectors, CLC affiliation and creation date; a reachable cross-tenant read is not made safe by the data being organization-level, so the route blocks release until a mandate and a scope are decided.

defectRegister.title: GET /api/organizations/[id]/descendants reads every organization whose hierarchy_path contains the path id inside withSystemContext, with no limit, after checking only that a session user exists, so any signed-in user receives the whole subtree of any organization (for a federation or the congress, every affiliate and local) with name, slug, type, parent id, hierarchy path and level, member count and status; the scope is the path id and never the caller organization, and an organization the caller does not belong to is not distinguished from one they do.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: Any signed-in user can call the route with the id of an organization that is not theirs: the only guard is the presence of a session user id, the lookup runs under withSystemContext (the union_eyes_system role that the 0108 row-level-security policy exempts), and the response returns the whole subtree of organizations with their hierarchy paths, member counts and status of that organization.

potentialImpact.description: A member or officer of one organization learns the identity, size and structure of organizations they have no relationship with; the 0108 policy states that a tenant sees only its own organization row, and this route discloses the whole subtree of organizations with their hierarchy paths, member counts and status outside that boundary.

releaseDisposition.justification: The route authenticates a user but never relates the caller to the requested organization, runs the read with the system role that bypasses tenant isolation, and returns the whole subtree of organizations with their hierarchy paths, member counts and status; a reachable cross-tenant read is not made safe by the data being organization-level, so the route blocks release until a mandate and a scope are decided.

defectRegister.title: GET /api/organizations/[id]/ancestors reads the hierarchy_path of the path organization and then its ancestor rows inside withSystemContext after checking only that a session user exists, so any signed-in user learns which federations and congress an organization they do not belong to is affiliated with (name, slug, type, level, status of each ancestor), and the response is the same empty list whether the organization is unknown, a root, or one the caller may not see.

The ancestors, children and analytics routes compare the raw path segment with a uuid column and the descendants route compares it with the hierarchy text array without validating its shape (the item route validates it, these do not): a segment that is not a uuid makes the database raise an unhandled error and a 500, and an unknown organization answers 200 with an empty list (ancestors, children, descendants) instead of 404, so a caller cannot tell an organization that does not exist from one with no relatives.

When the canonical bootstrap flag is not 1, GET /api/organizations/[id]/path checks only that a session user exists and then selects the organization named by the path uuid or slug, and every ancestor named by its hierarchy_path, through the shared db client with no withRLSContext, no withSystemContext, no membership check and no comparison with the caller organization: the result depends entirely on the row-level-security role of the connection (an unscoped tenant connection returns no rows, so the route answers empty for everyone; a connection the policy does not bind returns the name, slug, parent id, sector, jurisdiction and description of any organization and its ancestry), and only the canonical branch limits the path to the memberships of the caller and reports omitted ancestors.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: Any signed-in user calls /api/organizations/<uuid or slug>/path in the legacy mode: the handler authenticates the session user, queries organizations and the ancestors through the shared db client, and returns the path with name, slug, parent id, sector, jurisdiction and description of each organization found, with no check of the caller membership.

potentialImpact.description: A user of one organization can read the identity, jurisdiction, description and ancestry of another organization by id or slug whenever the connection role is not confined by the organizations row-level-security policy, and receives a silently empty path for their own organization when it is.

existingContainment.summary: In the canonical mode (UE_CANONICAL_BOOTSTRAP_V2 set to 1) the route returns getCanonicalOrganizationPath, which is limited to the memberships of the caller and reports the ancestors it omitted; the legacy branch has no such limit.

releaseDisposition.blockingCondition: The deployment runs with UE_CANONICAL_BOOTSTRAP_V2 unset or 0 and the DATABASE_URL role used by the shared db client is not confined by the 0108 organizations policy, so the legacy branch returns rows of organizations other than the caller own.
releaseDisposition.justification: The canonical branch is membership scoped, so the exposure exists only in the legacy mode and only if the connection role is not confined by the policy; both are runtime facts the route does not state. Where both hold the route discloses other tenants organizations to any signed-in user, so it blocks release under that condition.

defectRegister.title: GET /api/organizations/[id]/analytics checks only that a session user exists and takes the organization from the path id with no uuid validation and no membership check: it reads the organization name and type inside withSystemContext and counts its child organizations inside withSystemContext for any id, and then computes member totals, active members, new members this month, member growth rate, grievance totals, active, resolved and this-month counts, average resolution days and the grievances by status with statements filtered by that path id, so a signed-in user of any organization receives the analytics of any other organization on a connection whose row-level security does not confine the counts, and at least its name, type and child count when it does.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: Any signed-in user can call the route with the id of an organization that is not theirs: the only guard is the presence of a session user id, the lookup runs under withSystemContext (the union_eyes_system role that the 0108 row-level-security policy exempts), and the response returns the name, type, child organization count and (where the connection does not confine them) the member and grievance aggregates of that organization.

potentialImpact.description: A member or officer of one organization learns the identity, size and structure of organizations they have no relationship with; the 0108 policy states that a tenant sees only its own organization row, and this route discloses the name, type, child organization count and (where the connection does not confine them) the member and grievance aggregates outside that boundary.

releaseDisposition.justification: The route authenticates a user but never relates the caller to the requested organization, runs the read with the system role that bypasses tenant isolation, and returns the name, type, child organization count and (where the connection does not confine them) the member and grievance aggregates; a reachable cross-tenant read is not made safe by the data being organization-level, so the route blocks release until a mandate and a scope are decided.

defectRegister.title: The metric statements of GET /api/organizations/[id]/analytics run inside withRLSContext with no context map (the organization context of the session) while their organization_id predicate is the path id, and the child count runs under a nested system context: for an organization other than the caller own, a connection confined by the 0108 policy returns zero rows for the member and grievance counts, so the route answers 200 with zeros and a real child count that read as a measured figure of an organization whose data it could not see.

GET /api/organizations/[id]/analytics coalesces the average resolution days to 0 when no grievance has a resolution date, reports a member growth rate of 100 when the previous month count is zero and members exist, counts members without excluding soft-deleted rows, applies no role floor (any session user reaches it) and applies no minimum group size to the grievance status counts, so unmeasured values are presented as measured figures and a small organization status counts can identify the members involved.

The /api/organizations/[id]/access-logs route is crudRoutes over the organizations table (itemRoute true, orgScoped false) wrapped by requireOwnOrganizationItem: it never reads the cross_org_access_log table, applies none of the page, pageSize, resourceType, accessType, fromDate and toDate parameters the access log viewer sends, and answers with the organizations row of the caller own organization as {data: row} while the viewer reads logs, pagination and stats, so the viewer shows no log and no other organization access to the resources of the organization is ever reported.
