releaseDisposition.actualExposure: An officer of any organization that holds the commercial_reporting entitlement calls GET /api/reconciliation/process?runId=<uuid> and receives the reconciliation run with that id whichever organization owns it: the route checks the caller own financial mandate and then calls getReconciliationRun(runId), whose query filters on the run id alone.

potentialImpact.description: Another organization run record (period, invoice and payment counts, invoice and payment totals in CAD, variance, run-by user id and the billing period id) is returned to a caller outside that organization once its run id is known, with no organization predicate to refuse it.

releaseDisposition.justification: The mandate check proves only that the caller holds the finance:view duty in their own organization, the entitlement gate restricts the route to organizations that bought commercial_reporting but not to the owner of the run, the run id is a uuid supplied by the caller, and the service query has no organization condition; a reachable cross-tenant read is not contained by an identifier being hard to guess, so the route blocks release.

defectRegister.title: The reconciliation service (runReconciliation, resolveException, getReconciliationRun, listExceptions, requireReconciliation) imports the shared db handle and opens its own db.transaction without a tenant context, so the organization predicates written in each query (and absent from getReconciliationRun and requireReconciliation) are the only boundary unless the connection role is itself subject to row-level security, which the route files do not establish; the mandate check in the route runs in a separate withRLSContext transaction that the service does not join.

runReconciliation writes the run, matches and exceptions in db.transaction but calls auditLog (the application audit logger, which does not take the transaction handle) inside it, and resolveException updates the exception and then calls auditLog after the update committed, so the audit event is a separate write: a failed audit of a resolution or write-off leaves the status changed without the record (and in legacy mode the logger logs and swallows a database failure), and a run that later rolls back can leave its audit event behind.

POST /api/reconciliation/process inserts a new reconciliation_runs row and fresh exception rows on every call for the same period (no uniqueness, no supersede or correction of an earlier run), stores the billingPeriodId from the body without checking that the period belongs to the organization, and requireReconciliation(billingPeriodId), the guard that decides whether a period may be closed, filters the runs by period id alone with limit 1 and no order, so a run of one organization (or any earlier run) can satisfy the closure guard; the only caller of that guard is closeBillingPeriod, which no route calls.

runReconciliation records a fee_settlement match for each fee event that has a settlement batch id by copying the fee amount as both the source and the target amount with a variance of 0.00, without reading any settlement batch amount, so these matches are always reported as matched; it sums payments whose status is refunded into the payment total as if received; and the exception types duplicate_payment, missing_fee_event and orphaned_refund that the schema defines are never created, so the run reports totals and exception counts that do not test duplicates, missing fees or refunds.

POST /api/reconciliation/resolve sets an exception to resolved or written_off with the typed notes (an empty string is accepted) and the resolver id, and changes no invoice, payment or ledger row, so a write-off removes the exception from the open list without any financial effect or evidence; the service does not compare the resolver with the user who ran the reconciliation, no second approver is required, and the mandate check passes no participants to the segregation-of-duties rule.

GET /api/reconciliation/bank lists the reconciliation runs of the organization and GET /api/reconciliation/upload lists reconciliation exceptions; neither receives, parses or matches a bank statement (the upload route comment says the intake is reserved for future work), and no route records a bank transaction, so the paths named for bank reconciliation reconcile platform invoices and payments only.

GET /api/reconciliation/bank returns every run of the organization with no limit, and GET /api/reconciliation/upload splits the status query value on commas and casts it to the exception status enum without validation (and returns every matching exception unpaged), so an invalid status value reaches the database as an enum error and the lists grow without bound.

GET /api/rewards/export has no role check: after a session and the organization lookup it selects by organization alone and returns as a CSV download every award (recipient and issuer user ids, reason text), every wallet ledger row (user id, event type, credits, balance, memo) and every budget envelope of the organization to any member, while the wallet and redemption routes hold a member to their own rows.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: Any signed-in member of an organization calls GET /api/rewards/export?type=ledger, awards or budgets and receives a CSV of every row of the organization: all members user ids with their credit amounts, balances and memos, every award with recipient, issuer and reason, and every budget envelope; the route resolves the organization from the session and applies no role test and no relation between a row and the caller.

potentialImpact.description: Colleagues learn what each member earned and spent, the free-text reason and memo attached to each award and ledger entry, who recognised whom and the program budgets, which the wallet and redemption routes hold to the member own rows and which no source says members may see.

releaseDisposition.justification: The only guards are a session and an organization membership at any role, the queries select by organization alone and return the whole table as a download, and the sibling wallet and redemption routes show the intended own-row boundary; the data is personal to each member and the audience is undecided, so a signed-in member reaches every colleague record today and the route blocks release.

defectRegister.title: The CSV writer of GET /api/rewards/export quotes only values that contain a comma, a quote or a newline and does not neutralise a leading equals, plus, minus or at sign, so a free-text award reason or ledger memo that begins with a formula is written verbatim and is evaluated when an administrator opens the file in a spreadsheet.

GET /api/rewards/export returns the whole awards, ledger or budgets table of the organization in one response with no limit or date range, and records nothing about who exported what: the route writes no audit row and sits under no wrapper that does, so a bulk disclosure of member wallet data leaves no trace.

The anniversary task of POST /api/rewards/cron selects every organization member whose join date has today month and day and, for each, creates and issues a new Work Anniversary recognition award (credits applied by issueAward) with no check for an award already made for that member and year and no uniqueness on recipient, award type and date in recognition_awards, so the same call repeated on the same day, a scheduler retry or an overlapping run awards and credits the members again; the awards and credits are created in two separate transactions per member.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: The scheduler holder of CRON_SECRET calls POST /api/rewards/cron (task anniversaries or all); for every active organization the task selects every member whose join date falls on today and creates and issues a new Work Anniversary award with its credit amount, with no record or constraint that the award was already made, so a second call on the same day, a scheduler retry or an overlapping run awards and credits the same members again.

potentialImpact.description: Members receive the anniversary credits two or more times, the wallet ledger and program budget are charged each time, duplicate recognition awards appear in the member history and the export, and the credits are redeemable for provider goods, so a retry converts directly into spendable value.

existingContainment.summary: Only a caller with the cron secret reaches the task, and an anniversary award is issued only for an organization that has configured an automated Work Anniversary award type, which the route does not create.

evidence.quote: logger.warn('[Automation] No anniversary award type found', { orgId });

releaseDisposition.blockingCondition: An organization configures an automated Work Anniversary award type with a credit amount and the scheduler calls the cron route more than once on a day on which a member has an anniversary (a retry, an overlapping run, two schedulers, or a manual call).
releaseDisposition.justification: The route reaches no one without the shared secret and no award is made until an organization configures the automated type, so the harm is conditional; once an organization has done so, any repeat of the call on an anniversary day creates and credits a second award because recognition_awards has no uniqueness on recipient, type and day, and the credits are spendable, so the repeat path blocks release for any organization that uses anniversary awards.

defectRegister.title: The scheduled task of POST /api/rewards/cron loads the active scheduled automation rules of each organization, logs each one and increments processed without evaluating any schedule or issuing any award (the source comment calls it a placeholder), so the response reports rules processed for work that was not done.

The expiration task of POST /api/rewards/cron e-mails members whose earn ledger rows have an expires_at inside the next 7, 14 and 30 days (three overlapping windows run on every call, so a row expiring in 5 days is selected in all three), summing the earned credits of those rows and ignoring any spending; the call sites that write earn rows pass no expiresAt and no code was found that writes an expire entry, so today the task selects nothing and reports success with zero notifications, and once an expiry is set it would mail the same member up to three times per run with no sent record and with a credit count that does not reflect what was spent.

POST /api/rewards/cron returns success true with HTTP 200 for any task value (an unknown task executes nothing and returns an empty executed list), embeds a per-organization failure as an entry inside a successful response (processAnniversaryAwards returns success false with the error object instead of throwing, and a rejected organization is serialised as an Error object that JSON renders as empty), and wraps the expiration result, whose own success flag may be false, in the same success true, so a scheduler that checks the status code cannot see a failed run.

The proxy requires the x-cron-secret header for /api/rewards/cron and compares it with the CRON_SECRET value using !==, and the route then requires the same secret again in an Authorization bearer header (compared in constant time), so a scheduler must send the secret in two transports, a secret query parameter is documented in the route comment but not read, and the GET handler has no secret check of its own and depends on the proxy alone.

processAnniversaryAwards computes calculateAnniversaryCredits(yearsOfService) into a variable that is never used (the credit amount issued is the award type default), so a service-based credit scale is implied but not applied, and the reason text stored on every award and shown to the member reads with followed by the organization UUID instead of the organization name.

The rewards cron route and the wallet, redemption, automation, award and notification services import the shared db handle (and the cron route lists every active organization through it and runs raw SQL on organization_members) without a tenant context, and the wallet and redemption routes are wrapped by withRoleAuth, which sets no row-level-security context, so the organization and user predicates written in each query are the only boundary unless the connection role is itself subject to row-level security, which the route files do not establish.

Each anniversary award commits its create audit row in the award transaction and its issue audit row in a second transaction, but the cron run as a whole (organizations covered, members awarded, failures, warnings e-mailed) is written to no audit row, a failure between the two transactions leaves an approved award that is never issued and is not retried, and the expiration e-mails that leave the application are not recorded anywhere beyond a log line.

GET /api/rewards/redemptions validates the status query value against pending, ordered, fulfilled, cancelled and refunded (the cancellable states initiated and pending_payment are not in the list) and then never passes it to listUserRedemptions, so the filter has no effect and a member cannot ask for the redemptions that they are allowed to cancel; hasMore is the page length equal to the limit.

GET /api/rewards/redemptions returns the whole reward_redemptions row of each of the caller redemptions (listUserRedemptions uses findMany with no column list), including providerPayloadJson, which holds the shop provider checkout payload and the cancellation reason, so provider-side identifiers are returned to the member browser.

POST /api/rewards/redemptions parses the body with initiateRedemptionSchema into a variable that is never used and then cancels the redemption named by the id query value (refunding the credits), so a client that posts a new redemption receives a cancellation or a missing-id error, the schema validates fields that are ignored, and the cancel does not tell the shop provider that the checkout it may already hold has been cancelled.

GET /api/rewards/wallet reads the balance (the latest ledger row by created_at) and the ledger page in separate statements, so a ledger write between them returns a balance that does not match the page, takes limit and offset from parseInt of the query string without a NaN or negative check, and reports hasMore as the page length equal to the limit.

The report definition reads (the collection, the item and every path that is a copy of them) are the generic factory read at a member floor over the reports table: the table has no owner column the factory uses and the routes declare no ownerColumn, so any member of the organization receives every report definition of the organization, including definitions written by other users and definitions whose is_public flag is false, each with its whole config JSON that names data sources, fields and filter values, and no route under /api/reports reads is_public, so the flag restricts nothing.

The report definition writes store the config JSON from the request body as written: the column is an untyped notNull jsonb, no schema bounds its size or depth, and nothing at save time applies the contract of the report executor (a data source id of its registry, registry field ids, its filter operators, its allowed joins) or the allowlist of the execute route, so a definition that names an unknown source, a refused operator or a join to any table is stored and returned as a success that a later run would refuse or misread.

The /api/reports/[id]/execute and /api/reports/[id]/run routes are the same generic crudRoutes configuration over the reports table as the item route: neither imports ReportExecutor, reads a source table or loads the config of the report into an engine, so a GET answers the stored definition row (not a result), a PATCH rewrites the definition (including run_count and last_run_at, which no route ever advances) and answers success, and a DELETE at the administrator floor hard-deletes the report itself, so a caller or client that believes it is running or removing a run removes the report definition.

The /api/reports/[id]/share route is the same generic crudRoutes configuration over the reports table as the item route: it has no recipient, link, grant or share column, sends nothing and checks nothing, a PATCH that sets is_public true or false only stores a flag that no route reads, and a DELETE at the administrator floor, the natural verb to revoke a share, hard-deletes the whole report, so a share request is answered with success while nothing is shared, and a revocation destroys the report.

The /api/reports/templates route is the generic collection over the reports table with no template filter: a GET returns every report definition of the organization to any member, including custom, scheduled and private definitions that are not templates (the table has is_template and a template value of report_type and the route reads neither), and a POST stores a definition with is_template false unless the body sets it, so the list that the admin page labels templates is the whole definition table.

The /api/reports/builder and /api/reports/datasources/sample routes are the generic collection over the reports table: the builder answers a GET with the definition rows and a POST stores the posted body as a definition without applying the data source registry or the execute allowlist to it, and the data source sample route, which the data source explorer calls with sourceId and fieldId to preview values, ignores both parameters, reads no data source and returns a page of report definitions under a data key where the explorer reads a samples array, so a field preview is always empty and a POST to the sample route creates a report row.

The /api/reports/scheduled and /api/reports/scheduled/[id] routes are the generic CRUD configuration over the reports table, which has no schedule, recipient, delivery method, export format, next run or active column, while the scheduled report form posts reportId, scheduleType, scheduleConfig, deliveryMethod, recipients, exportFormat and isActive: none of those keys is a column, a create carries neither the notNull name nor the notNull config so it cannot insert a row, a pause or resume PATCH with an action key writes only updated_at and is answered with success, the list answers data and pagination where the page reads schedules, a DELETE hard-deletes a report row, and the scheduled reports cron answers 501, so no schedule, recipient list or delivery exists and the pause, resume and delete the page confirms change nothing about delivery.

POST /api/reports/execute validates the caller-supplied report configuration only for the fields, filters, grouping and sort (the joins are not read by the route) and the executor then builds the join from the caller: any registry table (claims, organization_members, claim_deadlines, dues_assignments) with any registry columns and an operator of =, !=, >, <, >= or <=, the select list qualifies a column with the caller-supplied field.table, and the only organization predicate of the statement is organization_id = the session organization on the base table, so a join such as claims INNER JOIN organization_members ON claims.id != organization_members.id selects id, status and created_at of the member rows of every organization, and claims.id != dues_assignments.id or claim_deadlines does the same for dues assignments and deadlines, up to the executor default limit of 1000 and to any limit the caller names, with whether the rows of other organizations are filtered resting wholly on database row-level security that the route does not set (a tenant transaction and the union_eyes_runtime role exist only when UE_CANONICAL_BOOTSTRAP_V2 is 1).

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: An officer of any organization posts a report configuration to /api/reports/execute with a join to another registry table on a non-equality operator and a select field qualified with the joined table: the executor adds organization_id equal to the session organization to the base table only and returns the joined-table rows of every organization (member ids, statuses and creation dates, dues assignment ids and statuses, claim deadline ids and statuses), subject only to whatever row-level security the connection role applies.

potentialImpact.description: An officer can read identifiers, statuses and dates of member, dues and deadline rows that belong to other organizations through a report join, and can use filters on joined columns to test values held by other organizations, because the organization predicate is attached to one table of a multi-table statement.

activationEvidence.quote: export const POST = withRoleAuth('officer', async (request: NextRequest, context) => {

existingContainment.summary: When UE_CANONICAL_BOOTSTRAP_V2 is 1 the wrapper runs the handler inside withRLSContext, which switches the transaction to the union_eyes_runtime role, and the migrations create direct organization policies for claims, organization_members and claim_deadlines, so the joined rows of other organizations would be hidden by the database; with the flag unset or 0 the statement runs on the pooled connection with no tenant context and nothing in the route or the executor limits the joined tables.

releaseDisposition.justification: The statement itself carries no organization predicate for any joined table and the join, the operator and the qualifying table come from the caller, so correctness of tenant isolation is delegated to row-level security that is active only in the canonical mode and that the route does not assert; a reachable path that returns rows outside the caller organization when the connection is not bound by the policy is not contained by a flag the source does not force, so the route blocks release until every table of the statement is held to the session organization in the query.

defectRegister.title: POST /api/reports/execute checks each filter against the route allowlist by filter.fieldId while the executor evaluates filter.fieldName when it is present (a registry column of any registry table, qualified or not), so a filter can name columns the route refuses as fields (claims.member_id, claims.assigned_to, organization_members.role, dues_assignments.amount) with the operators in and between that both layers accept, and use the row count and the selected rows as a test of what those columns hold; the route also never reads joins, having, limit, offset or the table qualifier of a selected field, and the executor accepts limit and offset from the caller (default 1000, no maximum), so one request can ask for an unbounded read and the rate limit of 30 per hour is the only bound.

POST /api/reports/execute accepts the filter operators equals, not_equals, contains, greater_than, less_than, between and in, while the executor implements eq, ne, gt, lt, gte, lte, like, ilike, in, not_in, is_null, is_not_null and between and skips any other operator without an error: a filter with equals, not_equals, contains, greater_than or less_than passes the route, is dropped by the executor, and the report is returned with its other conditions and no restriction from that filter, so a report configured for one status, type or period returns every claim or member row of the organization (up to the limit) with success true.

POST /api/reports/execute answers 200 with success false, no data and no row count when the executor fails (an unknown data source of the executor registry, a field or column the table does not have, a join the executor refuses or a database error), because the executor returns the failure as a value and the route copies only success, data, rowCount and executionTime, dropping the error text; the audit event of that run is logged with the event type success and the success flag in its details, an exception is logged as auth_failed with severity high, and a data source the route allowlist accepts but the executor registry does not (members, deadlines, grievances) fails this way for every caller.

POST /api/reports/execute returns the rows of the executed configuration to any caller whose role title is officer or above: the allowlist lets the caller select the email and status of every member of the organization (and claim numbers, types, statuses and dates of every claim), with no per-field authority, no classification or consent check, no row cap smaller than the caller limit and no suppression of small groups, and the only records are a logger line by logApiAuditEvent (user, data source, counts, no rows, no field list) and the generic wrapper record of the path, so what an officer extracted is not durably recorded and no institutional decision names the offices that may reproduce member or claim columns in a report.

GET /api/reports/datasources advertises four sources (claims, organization_members, claim_deadlines, dues_assignments) with fields that the execute route does not match: the route allowlist refuses claim_deadlines and dues_assignments (400) and accepts members, deadlines and grievances that the executor registry does not have, and the registry names columns that the tables do not define (organization_members first_name and last_name where the table has name, claims outcome where the table has resolution_outcome, claim_deadlines current_deadline where the table has due_date and original_deadline), so a report built from the registry as advertised is refused by the route or fails in the database and is answered 200 with success false.

GET /api/reports/datasources is wrapped in withApiAuth only and applies no role floor: any signed-in user with an organization receives the whole registry (table names, column names, types and the joinable tables, including member email, member id and dues amount columns) although running a report needs the officer role, and the organization it checks is the one on the user object, not one resolved for the query; the response contains no rows.

The signature request route reads the signers list from a multipart field with JSON.parse and no schema, and stores each signer name, e-mail address and user id exactly as the sender typed them, with no check that the user id belongs to the organization or to a person whose name or e-mail address matches; recordSignature then binds a signature only by requiring the signer row user id to equal the authenticated caller, so a sender can list their own user id with another person name and e-mail address, record the signature as that person (the audit trail row names the stored signer name and the sender-typed e-mail address as the actor), and when every signer row is signed the document is set to completed with no provider acknowledgment; the same local signing can complete a document that was sent through DocuSign or HelloSign without that provider ever being asked, so a signed or completed record states an identity and an act that no identified counterpart gave.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: Any authenticated user with an organization can create a signature document (withApiAuth sets no role floor) naming any signer text, list their own user id as a signer, sign it through the sign route, and the service marks the signer signed and the document completed with an audit row that attributes the signature to the typed name and e-mail address.

potentialImpact.description: A completed signature document and its audit trail record that a named person signed when the only actor was the sender, so an agreement, consent or acknowledgment can be shown as signed by someone who never saw it.

releaseDisposition.justification: Reachability needs only an authenticated session in an organization, the signer name and e-mail address are free text the sender controls, and the only identity binding is a user id equality that a sender satisfies by naming themselves; no verification of the typed identity, no counter-signature step and no provider acknowledgment is required before the document is completed, so the false attestation is available to every signed-in user.

defectRegister.title: The signature audit trail rows are plain inserts into signature_audit_trail: the hash_chain column is declared as a future link and AuditTrailService.log never sets it, nothing recomputes the stored file hash after creation or compares it at signing or completion, no row is signed or sealed, and the signer IP address comes from the first value of a client-supplied x-forwarded-for header, the geolocation from the request body and the signature image from any URL the signer posts; the audit route nevertheless returns the rows and, with format=report, a report that the service documents as generated for legal compliance, so a document status, a report and an audit trail are presented as evidence of an e-signature when none of their contents is verified or tamper-evident.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: The sender and every signer of a document can read the audit trail and the report; the rows are written by the application with caller-supplied IP address, user agent, geolocation and signature image URL and any database writer can alter them without a mismatch being detectable.

potentialImpact.description: An organization that relies on the report as proof of who signed, when and from where could present self-asserted and alterable records as legal evidence, and a counterparty or tribunal that tests them would find no hash chain, no verified identity and no sealed document.

releaseDisposition.blockingCondition: The audit report, a completed status or a stored signature is relied on or given to a counterparty, regulator or tribunal as evidence of an electronic signature, or the organization states that its signatures are legally valid.
releaseDisposition.justification: The harm needs reliance on the report as legal evidence, which no source in the repository decides or prevents, and the read is limited to the sender and the signers of a document; but the report and the trail are labelled for legal compliance while the chain column is unused and the evidence is self-asserted, so the route must not be used for that purpose until the institution names the validity basis and the records are sealed and verified.

defectRegister.title: The void path calls provider.voidEnvelope inside a try block whose catch is empty, before and outside the transaction that records the void, and then sets the document to voided and writes the document_voided audit row and the atomic audit row whether or not the provider voided the envelope; a DocuSign or HelloSign envelope that failed to void stays open and signable by its signers at the provider while the organization record, the audit trail and the PATCH response say voided, and the provider status sync then ignores the provider later reporting completed because a voided state is final.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: The sender of a document that was created through DocuSign or HelloSign can void it; the provider call is made first and its failure, including an expired credential or a provider outage, is discarded, after which the local record is voided and the success message is returned.

potentialImpact.description: A signer can complete an agreement at the provider that the organization has recorded and told the counterparty is voided, leaving the two records in conflict, and the organization record will not reflect the provider completion.

activationEvidence.quote: throw new SignatureAuthorityError("FORBIDDEN", "Only the sender of a document can void it");

existingContainment.summary: Only the person who sent the document can void it, and a completed, voided, declined or expired document cannot be voided, so the actor set is the senders of provider-backed documents.

releaseDisposition.blockingCondition: An organization configures a DocuSign or HelloSign credential and a sender voids a provider-backed document that a signer can still open at the provider.
releaseDisposition.justification: Without a configured external provider the void touches only the local record, and the sender-only rule limits who can trigger it, so the harm needs a live provider envelope; once one exists the swallowed failure leaves an open envelope that the organization records as voided, which is a false outcome that the route must not produce.

defectRegister.title: The signature request route has no role floor, no rate limit, no file size or type bound and no approval step: any authenticated user with an organization uploads a file in a multipart form, supplies a title, a description and a list of signers by name and e-mail address, and the service sends the file bytes, the signer names and e-mail addresses, the subject and the message to DocuSign or HelloSign under the organization provider credential, which then e-mails the typed addresses from the organization account, with no consent record for the recipients and no decision naming who may send documents for signature in the union name.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: Any member of any organization with an active session can call the POST; when DOCUSIGN_API_KEY or HELLOSIGN_API_KEY is set the default provider is the external one and the upload plus the typed recipients and message are transmitted to it and e-mailed to the typed addresses under the organization account.

potentialImpact.description: The organization signature account can be used by any member to send arbitrary documents and messages to arbitrary external addresses in the union name, disclosing the uploaded content and the recipient data to a third-party provider without any institutional approval or recipient consent, and consuming the provider quota.

releaseDisposition.blockingCondition: A DocuSign or HelloSign credential is configured for a deployment (the provider factory then prefers it over the internal stub) and the route is reachable by members.
releaseDisposition.justification: The external transmission exists only when a provider credential is configured, which is why the disposition is conditional, but once it is configured the route lets every authenticated user send content and messages to arbitrary recipients through the organization account, a PRIVACY_OR_CONSENT harm that the route, the service and the factory do not limit by role, approval, rate or recipient.

defectRegister.title: When no DocuSign or HelloSign credential is configured, or the caller sends provider internal, the provider factory returns InternalSignatureProvider, whose createEnvelope fabricates an envelope id and signing URLs that the service never stores or sends, whose status read always answers sent with no signers, and whose void and reminder methods are empty; the service nevertheless inserts the document as sent, writes the document_sent audit row, and the route answers success true, so signers who are external (no user id) receive nothing and can never sign because recordSignature rejects a signer with no user id.

The request route stores expiresAt, requireAuthentication and sequentialSigning on the document and the signing order on each signer, and recordSignature checks none of them: a signature is accepted after the expiry date, out of the signing order and without the authentication the sender required, and nothing sets the expired status for an internal document, so the options the sender chose and the audit text describe controls that do not operate.

The document status GET calls getDocumentStatus, which for any document that has a provider envelope and is not completed calls the provider and then updates the document status, the signer rows and the audit trail rows (each synchronization commits its own atomic audit under the system-provider-sync actor), so a read by any signer writes rows and makes an outbound provider call on every request, while a provider outage is swallowed and the stored status is returned as current.

The access check and the reads of signature documents, signers and audit rows run through the shared db import with no tenant context and no organization predicate (verifyDocumentAccess, getDocumentStatus, getDocumentAudit and generateAuditReport look the document up by id alone), and access rests on the sender or signer relationship, where a signer user id is whatever the sender typed with no check that it belongs to the sender organization, so a user of another organization named as a signer reads the document status, every signer row and the full audit trail of the organization, and isolation of these reads is not provable from the route or the service.

The document status returns every signer row with e-mail address, IP address, user agent, geolocation, signature image URL and provider identifiers, and the audit route returns every audit row and the report with actor e-mail addresses and IP addresses, to the sender and to every signer, so each signer, including an external counterparty who has a platform account, sees the network address and location of every other signer; the projection removes storage locations and extracted text only.

createSignatureRequest creates the provider envelope, which e-mails the signers, and uploads the file to document storage before the transaction that inserts the document, the signer rows, the audit trail rows and the atomic audit row, with no compensation, so a failure of the insert (for example a signer user id that is not a profile) leaves a live envelope that signers can complete and a stored file with no organization record or audit row, and the atomic audit proves only the local rows.

The document PATCH declares a zod schema (_signaturesDocumentsSchema) that requires a reason and is never applied; the handler reads action and reason from the raw JSON, accepts only the action void, and stores the reason text with no length bound in the document row, the audit trail row and the audit details.

The documents GET returns every document the caller sent and every document the caller must sign, with the complete signer row for the signing side, in one unpaginated response with no limit, so the response grows without bound with the number of requests.

The OAuth callback and the token refresh store the provider access token and refresh token in the text columns access_token and refresh_token of social_accounts exactly as received, with no encryption, no vault reference and no column-level protection (the calendar connection capability has a token-crypto module; nothing in lib/social-media or the social routes uses one), and the Meta, LinkedIn and X authorization requests ask for page management and posting, business_management and rw_organization_admin scopes, so a database read, backup or log exposure yields working publishing and administration credentials for every connected organization account.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: A steward who completes the OAuth flow causes the platform tokens to be written to the database in clear text; no route returns them (the accounts list selects a fixed field list), but every service that loads the row (publishing, refresh, delete) reads them and anyone with database or backup access reads them directly.

potentialImpact.description: A leaked token lets the holder publish, delete and administer the union public pages and read their data until each token is revoked, and the organization cannot tell from its own records that a token was used elsewhere.

defectRegister.title: The post route at the steward floor validates only shape and length, then publishSocialPost publishes the text, media URLs and link at once to every active account of the organization on each selected platform (the caller cannot choose an account, so every connected page of a platform receives the post), through the platform APIs, with no draft, review or approval state, no check of the content against any classification, no check that a linked document, a media file or a mention names a member who consented, and no record of who in the union decided to speak; the response reports the platform post ids and permalinks as published.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: Any steward of an organization with a connected active Facebook, Instagram, X or LinkedIn account can post any text, link and media URLs to every such account in one request, limited only by a 20-per-hour rate limit and the platform character limits.

potentialImpact.description: A single steward can make a public statement in the union name, including member names in mentions or media, bargaining or grievance content and links, on every connected public page with no approval, no consent check and no way to recall it other than a separate delete.

existingContainment.summary: The route requires the steward floor, a 20 per hour per-user rate limit and the per-platform character limits, and publishing needs an active connected account for the platform.

releaseDisposition.blockingCondition: An organization connects a Facebook, Instagram, X or LinkedIn account, after which any steward can publish to it.
releaseDisposition.justification: The harm needs a connected account and a steward, which limit who can act, but a steward floor is a role title and the union has recorded no decision on who may speak publicly or what may be posted; a public post cannot be reliably recalled, so the route must not publish without an approval and classification step once an account exists.

defectRegister.title: For an X post with media URLs the publisher checks only that the URL scheme is http or https (its comment says it validates the URL to prevent SSRF), then calls fetch(url) from the server with default redirect following, reads the whole body with arrayBuffer with no size, content type, host or address-range check, casts the response content-type header to an image or video type and uploads the bytes to the X media endpoint, so a steward can make the server request loopback, link-local, cloud metadata or private network addresses and any redirect target, and the response of whatever answers as an image or video is posted from the organization X account.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: A steward of an organization with a connected X account can include media_urls in the post request (up to ten http or https URLs validated by zod as URLs only); the server fetches each from its own network position before the upload.

potentialImpact.description: The server can be made to call internal services and metadata endpoints with GET requests, to download arbitrarily large bodies into memory, and to relay any image or video it can reach to a public account.

releaseDisposition.blockingCondition: An organization connects an X account and the application runs where internal or metadata addresses are reachable from the server.
releaseDisposition.justification: The scheme check blocks only non-http schemes and every other address is fetched, so the control named in its own comment is absent; exposure needs a connected X account and a steward, which makes it conditional, but within that set the server-side request is unrestricted and the only response filter is whatever the X media endpoint accepts.

defectRegister.title: The OAuth callback is a GET that exchanges the code, calls the platform to resolve the identity, and inserts or overwrites the social_accounts row (tokens, status active) with onConflictDoUpdate, so a state-changing request is reachable by a link, and the temporary oauth cookies are cleared before the state, user and organization are compared, so any request to the callback (a forged link or a replay) destroys the pending flow of a connection that is under way; the audit is a logApiAuditEvent call after the row is committed, which writes a log line and no audit row, and the first Facebook Page or LinkedIn organization the account lists is connected without the steward choosing one.

Initiating and completing a connection and listing the connected accounts call logApiAuditEvent with an object holding userId, organizationId, action, dataType, success and metadata cast through any, but that function logs only timestamp, userId, endpoint, method, eventType, severity and details from its argument, none of which these calls supply, so the log line carries the user id and undefined values and the action, organization, platform and record id are discarded; no audit row exists for connecting an organization publishing identity.

Any steward starts the OAuth flow for the organization, and the authorization requests ask for Meta pages_manage_posts, pages_manage_engagement, instagram_content_publish and business_management and LinkedIn w_organization_social and rw_organization_admin, which exceed what posting needs and give the stored token administrative rights over the page; the same floor refreshes and disconnects accounts, and no source names the office that may connect, replace or remove the union public identity.

The disconnect deletes the social_accounts row and its tokens and answers Account disconnected successfully even when the X token revocation throws (the catch is empty), and it never revokes Meta or LinkedIn tokens (the code comments that they need no explicit revocation), so a token that was exposed or that the union intended to cancel stays valid at the platform with no stored copy left to revoke later; the platform post removal for scheduled Facebook posts is not attempted.

The refresh route marks the account expired and writes a token_refresh_failed audit row on any exception, including a transient platform error or a missing refresh token, discards the error and answers a generic 500, and on success sets the account status to active whatever status it held (suspended or rate_limited included); the Meta branch refreshes the stored page token with the user long-lived token exchange.

publishPost inserts the social_posts row after each platform call, so a database failure after a successful platform post is caught as a platform failure and the live post has no row, no audit and a failed result; per-platform failures are caught inside the operation, so the performAuditedOperation outcome record says completed even when every platform failed, and the request answers 500 with the raw platform error text in results when none succeeded but 200 with partial results when some did; the intent and outcome audit is not committed with any data row.

scheduled_for is passed to a platform only for Facebook (scheduled_publish_time); the Instagram, X and LinkedIn branches post immediately, yet the row is inserted with status scheduled, the requested time and no published time, so a post the steward scheduled is live at once while the record says it is waiting, and hashtags and mentions are stored on the row but sent to no platform, link_title and link_description reach only LinkedIn, and campaign_id is dropped.

The post create schema accepts campaign_id and the handler assigns it to an unused variable, the service insert has no campaign column, so no social_posts row ever has a campaign id; the campaign list metrics, the campaign analytics, the post analytics filter by campaign_id and the CSV campaign export therefore count zero posts for every campaign, and the delete guard that refuses to delete a campaign with posts can never fire.

No route, job or service writes social_analytics rows or the engagement counters of social_posts: fetchAnalytics has no caller and every platform branch of it is an empty block with a comment that the transformation is not implemented, the publish insert leaves impressions, reach, likes, comments and shares at their zero defaults, so the analytics read, the post performance read, the campaign metrics and the export answer 200 with empty or zero figures labelled as impressions, reach and engagement, and the summary averages are computed from those zeros.

The campaign analytics read builds platform_metrics and the timeline from post fields named impressions, engagement, likes, comments, shares and engagement_rate, which its select does not return (it selects impressionsCount and the other count fields), so those platform figures are zero or NaN-guarded to zero even when posts carry counts, goal_progress is a constant undefined, and the clicks total is a constant zero.

The campaign create schema accepts goals and status, checks the goals (metric and a positive target), then stores neither: the insert writes no goal columns and sets status to the literal active, requires at least one platform although the schema marks platforms optional, and the response is a success carrying the campaign row, so a steward is told that goals were recorded for a campaign that has none.

The campaign update reads name, description, platforms, dates, hashtags, target audience and status from the raw JSON with no schema, writes any of them (status, a platforms array of any strings, hashtags of any type), calls split on the date values so a non-string answers 500, and a status outside the enum fails in the database as a generic 500.

The analytics DELETE handler writes nothing and exports posts, account analytics or campaigns as CSV or JSON for the date range at the member floor, with no row limit, no rate limit and no audit record; the CSV writer does not neutralise values that start with equals, plus, minus or at, and it looks each cell up by a key derived from the header text, so the campaign export leaves the campaign name, impressions, engagement, likes, comments, shares and clicks columns blank and the account export leaves followers blank, and a zero value is written as blank.

The handler loads the campaign or post by id alone through the shared db import (the post lookup joins the account without an organization predicate) and compares the organization afterwards, answering 403 for another organization row and 404 for a missing one, so isolation of the lookup rests on the later comparison rather than the query and a caller can tell whether a campaign or post id exists in another organization.

limit and offset are parseInt of the raw query string with no number check, no minimum and no maximum, and are passed to the query, so a caller can request an arbitrarily large page, a negative value that the database rejects as a 500, or NaN.

The post delete asks the platform to remove the post and then updates the local row to deleted, so a failure of the local update after a successful platform removal leaves a row that says published for a post that no longer exists, a platform failure leaves the row published and returns only a generic 500, and the intent and outcome audit records are not committed with the row change.

The social media feed route is the generic CRUD factory configured over the communications campaigns table at member floor read and steward floor write, so the feed answers with campaign rows (name, subject, body, segment query, audience count, delivery statistics, status) instead of social posts, readable by any member including drafts and the audience query, while the feed widget expects platform, publishedAt, mediaUrls and hashtags and calls the deprecated v2 path; POST inserts a campaign row, not a social post, and publishes nothing.

Every GET over steward_assignments (the stewards collection and the stewards/[id] item) is configured at readRole member, and the table has no user, member, email or phone column by those names (its contact columns are workPhone, personalPhone, preferredContactMethod and availabilityNotes), so the low-role guard opens the read: any member of the organization, not only a steward or officer, receives the steward assignment rows with the personal phone number, work phone number, preferred contact method, availability notes, free-text notes, the grievance id of a case-based assignment, the appointer, tenure and training dates, and the unit, worksite and shift coverage, with no field projection and no read audit.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: Any member of an organization, whatever their role, calls GET /api/stewards or GET /api/stewards/<id>: readRole is member, the generic factory scopes the rows to the session organization and, because steward_assignments has none of the owner or personal column names the low-role guard looks for, applies no owner condition, and it returns the whole row (up to 100 per page) including personal_phone, availability_notes, notes and grievance_id.

potentialImpact.description: A member, including one who is the subject of a grievance the steward handles, reads the personal telephone number and availability notes of every steward and the grievance each case-based assignment is linked to; a steward who gave a work number to members has also given every member a personal number and free-text notes, and the grievance link reveals which member or case a steward is assigned to.

existingContainment.summary: The factory adds an organization predicate from the session organization, so only the rows of the caller own organization are read; nothing narrows them to a steward, an officer, a coverage area or a set of permitted fields, so the exposure is every steward row of the organization to every member.

releaseDisposition.justification: The routes serve personal contact data and free-text notes about a union representative, and a grievance link, to every authenticated member at the lowest role floor with no field projection; the tenant predicate keeps other organizations out but does not limit a same-organization reader, and no source establishes that members are the intended audience of the personal phone, the notes or the grievance link, so the read blocks release until the institution names the readers and the permitted fields.

defectRegister.title: The stewards and stewards/[id] routes are crudRoutes over steward_assignments: GET returns assignment rows, POST, PATCH and DELETE are refused with 403 because the governance list holds the table read-only, no other route appoints, confirms or ends a steward, and the only code that inserts an assignment row is assignSteward in the steward assignment service (a grievance assignment that sets the type to steward, writes no audit record and bumps a caseload counter on the separate stewards table) which no route calls, so the route names promise a steward directory with appointment and the source offers a read of per-case assignment rows and no way to create the directory.

The stewards collection and item routes configure writeRole steward over steward_assignments and the item route exports PATCH and DELETE with no blocked fields; the only thing that stops a steward from creating, rewriting or archiving any steward assignment (type, appointer, tenure, coverage, notes) is the presence of steward_assignments in the READ_ONLY list of the CRUD governance file, so a role title at the steward floor would become the authority to appoint stewards the moment that list changes.

The survey form tells the member that submitting anonymously means their name will not be visible to their representative, and the submit route stores isAnonymous on the survey row, but no query, service function or route reads the flag: the survey row keeps member_id and the rating and the free text whatever the flag says, the representative performance and ranking routes aggregate anonymous and named responses together, and a representative with one completed survey is returned that one response as an average, so an anonymous response is not anonymous to a steward who knows which claim the representative handled.

GET /api/satisfaction/lro/<lroId> returns the six rating averages, the overall average and the recommend rate of any representative id the steward types in, and GET /api/satisfaction/rankings returns and ranks every representative of the organization who has a completed survey, at the steward floor, with no minimum number of responses, no check that the id is a representative of the organization or the caller, no control over which steward may read the performance of which representative, and no read audit.

getLroPerformance turns a null average into zero (n = parseFloat(v ?? 0)) and computes the overall average as the mean of six values that may all be zero, so GET /api/satisfaction/lro/<lroId> for an id that is not a representative, or that has no completed survey in the organization, answers 200 with totalSurveys 0, six averages of 0, an overall average of 0 and a recommend rate of 0, which reads as a representative rated 0 out of 5 and not as no data.

POST /api/satisfaction (described in its header as an administrator action and in its OpenAPI text as creating a survey for a closed claim) is configured at the steward floor and selects only memberId and assignedTo from the claim: it never reads the claim status, so a survey can be created for an open claim, and when the claim has no assignedTo the lroId in the body is accepted as any string with no check that it names a representative of the organization, so a survey can be created that asks the member to rate a person who did not handle the claim.

GET /api/satisfaction passes only the session user id to getPendingSurveys, which filters satisfaction_surveys on member_id and status pending with no organization predicate and returns the whole rows, so a person who is a member of two organizations receives the pending surveys of both (claim id, representative id, sent time) whichever organization the session is acting in.

The SCIM 2.0 users route authenticates only a browser session at the administrator floor (withApi auth required, minRole admin) and reads neither scim_configurations (bearer token, token hash, expiry, enabled flag, deprovision action, attribute mapping) nor scim_events_log, so an identity provider that presents the long-lived bearer token the schema describes cannot call it, no token is issued, checked, expired or rotated by any route, no SCIM provisioning event is logged, and the route offers only list and create with no get, replace, patch or delete of a user, no groups and no service provider configuration, so a deprovision cannot be sent at all.

GET /api/scim/v2/<organizationId>/Users selects every organization_members row of the organization with no deleted_at and no status condition, slices the page in memory after loading the whole roster, and maps active to member.status equal to active alone, so a member who was removed (deleted_at set) while the status column still reads active is listed and reported as an active user with name and e-mail address, a count that is not a number (count=abc) makes the slice end NaN and the page empty, and a count of zero or less is accepted.

POST /api/scim/v2/<organizationId>/Users inserts an organization_members row whose user_id is the userName string from the body (the membership key that getUserRoleInOrganization matches against the session user id), with the e-mail taken from the body, the role fixed to member and the status active immediately: the identity provider subject is never read, the person does not accept, the userName may be any string including the identifier of an existing user of another organization (who is then made an active member of this one), and a provisioned person whose session user id differs from the userName string can never match the row, while a removed member with the same user id answers 409 as an existing user.

The SCIM create route reads the body with an unguarded request.json() and a type cast instead of a schema: malformed JSON or an emails value that is not an array raises a plain error that withApi answers as a 500, a userName that is not a string passes the presence check and reaches the insert, and no length or format bound is applied to userName, name or e-mail.

PUT /api/settings/organization merges whatever object the administrator sends as body.settings, with no key allow-list and no value validation, into the organizations.settings JSON that other code reads as authority: services/clc/per-capita-calculator reads settings.perCapitaRate (an organization with a rate of 0 or less is skipped) and settings.remittanceDay to compute the per-capita amount an organization with a parent owes that parent, lib/services/entitlements reads settings.credits and settings.nextCreditRenewal as the credit balance that checkEntitlement tests before a credit-requiring AI feature, and the twilioPhoneNumber key attributes inbound text messages, so an organization administrator can set their own remittance rate and day, credit balance and renewal date directly, and the audit row lists only the names of the fields written (settings, name, shortName, provinceTerritory), never a value.

releaseDisposition.actualExposure: An administrator of any organization (minRole admin) sends PUT /api/settings/organization with {"settings":{"perCapitaRate":"0.01","credits":1000000}}: the route merges the object into the stored settings JSON of the session organization in a tenant transaction and commits an organization.settings_update audit row that names the field settings but not the values, and the per-capita calculator and the entitlement check read those keys back on their next call.

potentialImpact.description: An organization administrator can lower or zero the per-capita rate (a rate of 0 removes the organization from the monthly remittance run, a low rate shrinks the amount computed as owed to its parent body) and can set the credit balance and renewal date that the entitlement check reads, so the parent body and the platform operator, who are not the writer, receive an amount the software computed from a value the payer wrote; the audit row does not record the values, so the change cannot be reconstructed.

existingContainment.summary: The caller must hold the administrator role and the update is scoped to the organization id of the session, so one organization cannot write another organization row; nothing limits which keys the administrator writes or which organization reads them for billing and remittance.

releaseDisposition.justification: The remittance amount lands on a party other than the writer (the parent body that the per-capita calculator remits to) and is reached by one administrator request with no allow-list, no value validation and no value in the audit record; the administrator role floor limits who can do it but not what it affects, the monthly job that reads the rate is source that runs for every organization with a parent, and no source names the administrator as the owner of the remittance rate or the credit balance, so the route blocks release until the keys the administrator may write are decided and enforced.

defectRegister.title: The platform settings page saves sessionTimeout, mfaEnforcement, passwordMinLength, requireMixedCase, requireSymbol, rateLimitPerMin and webhookUrl into the organization settings JSON through this route, which answers {updated:true}, and the settings page reads them back with defaults (mfaEnforcement admins_only, passwordMinLength 12), but no authentication, session, password, rate-limit or notification code found in the application reads those keys, so an administrator who sets multi-factor enforcement or a password policy is told the setting is saved while nothing enforces it.

PUT /api/settings/organization takes the body without a schema, accepts an empty string or an unbounded string as name, shortName and provinceTerritory, reads the current settings JSON with the shared database handle outside the transaction that writes the merge (so two concurrent saves overwrite each other keys), answers a missing body or organization as a plain error that withApi turns into a 500, and GET answers 200 with organization null for an organization row that does not exist.

handleInboundSms attributes an inbound text message to the organization whose settings JSON holds the called number under twilioPhoneNumber, selecting with limit 1 and no ordering or uniqueness, and the organization settings route lets any organization administrator write that key, so an administrator who stores the number of another organization makes the lookup ambiguous and the inbound message body and sender number can be stored in the conversation table of the wrong organization.

The security events route is configured for readRole and writeRole security_manager with a header comment that describes a privileged reader and a closed forgery path, but security_events is in the DENIED list of the CRUD governance file, so assertCrudRead and assertCrudWrite answer 403 to every caller including a security manager; the privileged reader of the table is the security dashboard page, which checks hasMinRole security_manager and reads the table with SQL under a system context, so the API the comment describes does not exist and the integrity rule for who may author a security event is held only by the governance list.

The storage/usage and storage/cleanup routes are crudRoutes over cms_media_library: GET returns the media library rows of the organization (file name, file url, type, size, folder, tags, uploader) at the member floor, and neither route sums file sizes, reads a quota, compares a file with the references to it or deletes anything, so a caller expecting storage usage receives a page of rows and a caller expecting a cleanup triggers none; the cms_media_library table is read and written by no code other than these two routes and the upload route.

POST /api/storage/usage and POST /api/storage/cleanup insert a cms_media_library row from the whole request body at the steward floor: no file is received or checked, so file_url (any string, including an external address), file_size, mime_type, uploaded_by (any profile user id) and folder are whatever the caller writes, and a library entry can point at a file that does not exist, at an address outside the application storage, or be attributed to another person.

The support/metrics and support/sla routes are crudRoutes over in_app_notifications: GET returns notification rows (user id, title, message, type, action label and url, data, read flag) and POST inserts one, and no route reads or computes a ticket count, response time, resolution time or service-level figure, so a caller expecting support metrics or SLA compliance receives unrelated notification rows; the figures themselves are computed by getTicketMetrics and getSLAMetrics in the support service over support_tickets, and no route calls that service.

GET /api/support/metrics and GET /api/support/sla hold a caller below steward to their own in_app_notifications rows, but any steward or higher role reads the notifications of every user of the organization (title, message, action url and the data object), unbounded by any relationship to the recipient and without a read audit, so notifications that name a member, a case or a grievance are readable beyond the member they were addressed to.

POST /api/support/metrics copies the body into an in_app_notifications row at the steward floor with no check that the user id is a member of the organization (the sibling POST /api/notifications makes that check), with a caller-written title, message and action url and no sender stored, so a steward can store a notification with an arbitrary link for any user id string and it appears to the recipient as a message of the application.
